BMC Infectious Diseases (2021) 21: 145 DOI: 10.1186/s12879-020-05716-z

Abstract

Background

Zambia has experienced a rapid increase in COVID-19 cases since March 2020. Lusaka is the epicentre of the Zambian outbreak with a case rate 2.6-fold higher than the national average. A large proportion of Zambian cases are asymptomatic. The aim of this study was to estimate the prevalence of SARS-CoV-2 infection in the Lusaka Metropolitan area, and assess the impact of different testing strategies on the control of the outbreak.

Methods

Mathematical models were fitted to the available data on the Zambian outbreak. These models were used to estimate the proportion of the Lusaka population that was infected by 20 April 2020, under different assumptions about the true case fatality ratio (CFR), and the prevalence of asymptomatic infection. The models were also applied to assess the impact of different testing strategies on outbreak control, assuming a testing capacity of 5000 tests per day.

Results

Our results indicate that a true CFR of 1.7% and an asymptomatic proportion of 87.1% provided the best fit to the data. Although this low CFR likely reflects the impact of limited access to healthcare, it also suggests that the majority of Lusaka residents have or will become infected. Estimating

of the basic reproductive number (R0) for SARS-CoV-2, the virus that causes COVID-19, in different scenarios in Senegal has found that the number can be reduced to below one if physical distancing is maintained and hygiene practices improved.

Senegal has to date recorded 5,402 cases of COVID-19 and 103 deaths due to the virus.

However, the number of new cases has recently declined, suggesting that measures taken by the government are working.

Ousmane Cissé and colleagues wanted to explore how effective the measures taken by the Senegalese government are at reducing the reproductive number R0, a measure of how quickly an infection spreads through a population.

They used mathematical modelling to estimate R0 for Senegal based on three different scenarios: the situation before the government implemented control measures; a situation where control measures are being implemented; and a situation where control measures are being relaxed.

The researchers found that R0 was high (estimated at 2.2) before control measures were introduced and that the number of infections would have increased 2.2-fold each day if no control measures were put in place.

However, if the control measures are being implemented, the study estimates that R0 is currently 1.8.

If the control measures are relaxed, the study estimates that R0 is 2.2 and increasing.

The study also found that the more effective the contact tracing and isolation of contacts is, the lower the number of new infections.

The researchers found that if contact tracing and isolation is 90% effective, R0 is reduced to 1, and if it is 50% effective, R0 is 1.4.

“Contact tracing and isolation are crucial to reduce R0 to below one and stop the epidemic,” the team states.

The study also found that improving hand hygiene reduces the number of new infections, but face masks are not necessary if good hygiene is observed.

The researchers state: “Our findings suggest that control strategies should primarily target improving hand hygiene and physical distancing while contact tracing and isolation should be implemented to further reduce the number of new infections to below one.”

They add: “These results underline the need for ongoing and effective implementation of control measures and highlight the importance of considering the local epidemiological context when designing and evaluating control strategies.”

Ousmane Cissé et al.

English: Background: Buruli ulcer (BU) is a neglected tropical disease caused by Mycobacterium ulcerans. Although rarely reported in Africa, BU has been consistently reported from the DRC, where a recent increase in incidence has been observed.
English: Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of all consecutive patients with BU admitted to a tertiary care hospital in Kinshasa between January 2015 and September 2020. We extracted demographic, clinical, and microbiological data from patients’ medical records. We used the Cochran-Armitage trend test to identify if there was a significant trend in the annual percentage change in incidence of BU over time and Fisher’s exact test to identify if there was a significant difference in the proportion of patients testing positive for COVID-19 between 2015–2019 and 2020.

The model incorporates the asymptomatic and symptomatic classes and assumes that infected asymptomatic individuals are as infectious as infected symptomatic individuals. Parameter values are estimated from literature and data collected from the ongoing COVID-19 outbreak in Zambia. The model shows that the outbreak can be controlled through active isolation of infected but asymptomatic individuals. It takes approximately 200 days to bring the outbreak under control through active isolation of infected but asymptomatic individuals. However, to avoid a large peak in the number of hospitalized individuals, testing should be initiated approximately 50 days before the expected onset of the peak. The model can be used to assess the impact of changes in the control strategy and to guide the design of a control plan for SARS-CoV-2 outbreak in Lusaka Province of Zambia.

Under the best-case scenario, we estimate that the active isolation strategy would lead to the avoidance of 1,277 deaths and 37,337 total COVID-19 cases. However, it would also lead to the identification and active isolation of 1,970,481 individuals, mostly without COVID-19, which would have resulted in 2,238 deaths and 131,810 total cases if the government had not intervened. We estimate that the total cost of the active isolation strategy would be 5.6 million USD, or 18.5% of the 2019 GDP of Zambia.
We find that the active isolation strategy would not be beneficial in the long run. It could only help reduce the number of deaths and total cases under very specific conditions that are highly unlikely to be met. Even if these conditions are met, the model predicts that the strategy would come at a very high cost. The model also predicts that the strategy would lead to large-scale social unrest and economic decline. The predicted economic decline would lead to a 9.5% reduction in the 2020 GDP of Zambia, a 21.5% reduction in government tax revenue, a 50% reduction in foreign direct investment, and a 90% reduction in remittance income.

samples.hyp:
The recent success of polygenic scores (PGS) in predicting individuals’ complex traits from their genotypes has sparked interest in their use for identifying individuals with increased risk of complex diseases. However, most of these studies have been conducted in European populations, and it is not clear to what extent these scores generalize to populations outside of Europe, especially those outside of Europe and the Americas. Here, we examine the generalizability of PGS for 34 complex traits from the Peninsula and Island Scotland (P&I) study, a large European ancestry cohort study in the UK, to 5 non-European populations in sub-Saharan Africa (Niger, Tanzania, Uganda, Zambia, and Zimbabwe) with small amounts of European ancestry. We show that scores trained on European individuals overestimate risk in African individuals, with the extent of overestimation depending on trait heritability and ancestry proportions. We also show that training the PGS on European and African individuals together produces scores that generalize better to African individuals with no European ancestry. These results highlight the importance of considering both genetic and non-genetic factors when evaluating PGS in diverse populations.

The genetic basis of disease is not the same in different ethnic groups. The impact of this on genetic testing is discussed.

The human genome is incredibly complex and is only just beginning to give up its secrets. We still have an incomplete understanding of the normal variation that exists between people and the small percentage of the genome that differs between individuals is associated with genetic disease. As we uncover the genetic basis of disease, it is important to establish whether the genetic risk factors identified in one ethnic group are relevant to other ethnic groups.

Here, we focus on genetic disease in people of African ancestry, an understudied group that is at high risk of developing genetic disease. Genetic risk in this group has only just started to receive attention with the development of new large-scale genotyping arrays that now include enough African samples to generate meaningful statistics.

It has long been known that the genetic basis of disease is not the same in different ethnic groups. Early studies of sickle cell disease, which is caused by a genetic mutation in the haemoglobin gene, showed that protection from malaria was a significant contributor to the high prevalence of this genetic disorder in sub-Saharan Africa. More recently, studies of genetic disorders have highlighted the need to consider the ethnic background of patients when interpreting genetic test results. This is not always done in clinical practice, leading to misinterpretation of test results in people of African ancestry. For example, the genetic disorder Krabbe’s disease is caused by a mutation in the GALC gene and symptoms include ataxia, muscle weakness and visual failure. This was only discovered on a second round of testing when genetic material from brain cells was analysed.

The PRS is a number representing the probability that an individual will have a particular disease, based on the combined effect of multiple genetic variants that are each associated with a small increased risk.

In the case of breast cancer, each variant is likely to only slightly increase a woman’s risk, but with hundreds or thousands of variants considered, the PRS score can accurately reflect her genetic risk. The score essentially “stratifies” people into different risk groups, and in the case of breast cancer, this has shown that a woman in the top 10% of the risk distribution is likely to have a one in three chance of developing the disease by the age of 70.

For the current study, the researchers trawled through genetic data from a number of large health studies to identify thousands of genetic variants that have been previously associated with a range of different diseases. They then selected 54 of these variants that had been consistently replicated across different studies and populations and are known to affect the function of 261 different genes.

The team then used this information, together with data on the affected individuals’ disease status and age, to calibrate the score against the diseases studied. They tested the accuracy of the score at predicting disease in two independent groups of individuals.

samples.src: Evaluation of Visual and Cytology Screening in Preventing Cervical Intraepithelial Neoplasia and Cervical Cancer in Namibia
samples.ref: Kimanta Gwajin Gani da kuma na Tsarin Ƙwayoyin Halitta da na Dabba a Wajen Hana Rashin Daidaituwa na Mahaifa da kum Kansar Mahaifa a Namibiya
samples.hyp:
This study evaluated the performance of visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA) with or without human papillomavirus (HPV) testing, and cervical cytology for cervical screening in Namibia, a country with few resources and a high prevalence of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and HPV.
Ninety women with positive VIA and/or cytology results were enrolled in the triage. Of these, 73% (n = 66) had CIN on repeat colposcopy and biopsy. The positive VIA and/or cytology results were significant predictors of CIN and cervical cancer with areas under the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve of 0.891 (95% CI = 0.81–0.97) and 0.955 (95% CI = 0.93–0.98), respectively. VIA positive for CIN was 71% sensitive (95% CI = 56%–83%) and 82% specific (95% CI = 70%–90%). The sensitivity and specificity of cytology were 85% (95% CI = 73%–93%) and 57% (95% CI = 44%–68%), respectively. The sensitivity and positive predictive value of HPV DNA testing were 66% (95% CI = 51%–78%) and 72% (95% CI = 56%–84%), respectively. The negative predictive value was 17% (95% CI = 9%–29%). The area under the ROC curve was 0.637 (95% CI = 0.5–0.72). Concomitant testing with VIA and cytology improved sensitivity to 97% with a specificity of 48%.
VIA with or without HPV testing identifies women with high-grade CIN and cervical cancer in a resource-limited setting. Triage with VIA and cytology improves the sensitivity of the test. However, the low specificity of cytology and the limited sensitivity and positive predictive value of HPV testing require caution in the use of these tests and highlight the need for validation in larger samples from population-based screening.

Citation: Wright P, Burt A, Cutland A, Pollock K, Skirrow H, Tintutlini T, et al. (2016) Evaluation of Visual and Cytology Screening in Preventing Cervical Intraepithelial Neoplasia and Cervical Cancer in Namibia. PLoS ONE 11

The aim was to determine the prevalence of HPV infection and cervical cancer risk factors among women attending a gynecology clinic in Windhoek, Namibia. A cross-sectional study was conducted among 369 women aged 30–69 years attending a gynecology clinic between March and December 2013. Written informed consent was obtained from each participant. Demographic data and cervical cytology were collected. Concomitantly, a blood sample was obtained to determine HPV infection by PCR and HPV16/18 serology. Univariate and multivariate analyses were conducted to determine the association between risk factors and HPV infection. Of the 338 women tested for HPV DNA, 36 (10.6%) were positive. HPV16/18 seropositivity was low (2.8%). HPV infection was more prevalent in women with less than primary school education, in women living in urban areas, and in Khoe women. In the multivariate analysis, only living in urban areas remained associated with HPV infection (adjusted prevalence ratio 2.40; 95% CI 1.32–4.36). The low prevalence of HPV infection and cervical cancer risk factors among women attending a gynecology clinic in Windhoek, Namibia, is concerning. The high risk of cervical cancer among Khoe women should prompt the implementation of cervical cancer screening in this ethnic group.

Keywords: Human papillomavirus infection; cervical cancer; risk factors; Namibia.

However, VIA is not widely available in low-resource settings. Cryotherapy is available in these settings and has the added benefit of treating cervical dysplasia. This study aims to compare VIA and cryotherapy for the treatment of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) in a low-resource setting.
A single-center study was conducted in a tertiary care facility in a low-resource setting. Women with CIN2 or CIN3 diagnosed by VIA were randomized to treatment with VIA or cryotherapy. Patients were followed up for recurrence of CIN after treatment. The primary outcome was recurrence of CIN at 6 months after treatment. Secondary outcomes included treatment-related adverse events and comparison of the efficacy of VIA and cryotherapy in the treatment of CIN2 and CIN3 lesions.
A total of 95 patients were recruited. The mean age was 34.2 years. Of these, 44 patients were randomized to VIA and 51 to cryotherapy. The recurrence rate at 6 months was similar between the two groups (VIA, 16.4%; cryotherapy, 13.7%; P = 0.6). The adverse event profile was similar except for a higher rate of anal pain in the cryotherapy group (7.8%) than in the VIA group (0%; P = 0.02). More CIN3 lesions were completely resolved in the VIA group than in the cryotherapy group (85.7 vs. 61.8%; P = 0.01). In a sensitivity analysis, the recurrence rate at 6 months for VIA and cryotherapy was 15.2% and 13.3%, respectively.
The results of this study show that the efficacy of cryotherapy and VIA is similar for the treatment of CIN in a low-resource setting. Both treatment modalities are effective for the treatment of high-grade CIN. VIA is associated with fewer treatment-related adverse events. However, both treatment modalities are safe and effective for the treatment of high-grade CIN. Larger studies are required to validate these findings.
Keywords: Cryotherapy; Episodic acid; Low-resource setting; Treatment; VIA; Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN); Human papillomavirus (HPV)

We aimed to evaluate the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of human papillomavirus (HPV) testing, visual inspection of the cervix with acetic acid (VIA), and visual inspection of the cervix with potassium hydroxide (KOH) for cervical pre-cancerous lesions, and to estimate the impact of different screening strategies on the incidence of cervical cancer in Rwanda. We built a mathematical model to describe cervical cancer and its precursors, and compare the lifetime incidence of cervical cancer under different screening strategies, in terms of life expectancy adjusted to age, sex, and cancer incidence of the Rwandan population. The model considered different screening strategies, comprising primary HPV screening, VIA, and KOH, with or without triage, and secondary screening with cervical biopsy. We calculated the number of deaths and quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) avoided, the number of screen positives, and costs per screening strategy. The effectiveness of HPV testing was assumed to be similar as in developed countries, and the effectiveness of VIA and KOH was estimated in a previous study. The costs of screening and treating cervical pre-cancerous lesions, and the number of screen positives to be managed, were taken from a previous study in Rwanda. We found that screening with HPV testing in single-visit screening approaches, with or without VIA as secondary test, was more effective than VIA or KOH, avoiding 58 additional deaths and 1499 additional QALYs at a cost of 530 US dollars per screening done in women aged 30 years. Screening with HPV testing was the most cost-effective strategy, with a cost-effectiveness ratio of 80 US dollars per QALY gained. A screening interval of ten years was sufficient to reach the same level of cervical cancer prevention as screening every three years, with the same number of screen positive results to be managed. Screening with HPV testing, or with VIA as secondary test, was more effective than current practice in Rwanda, avoiding 22 additional deaths and 506 additional QALYs at a cost of 166 US dollars per screening done in women aged 30 years. Conclusion: Screening for cervical pre-cancerous lesions in Rwanda should include HPV testing in single-visit screening approaches, with or without VIA as secondary test. Screening interval could be ten years and still maintain a high level of effectiveness.

In the setting of hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)-positive individuals have been shown to have worse outcomes than uninfected individuals. However, it is unclear whether this is also true for HBV/HIV coinfection compared to HBV monoinfection. Therefore, South African patients were followed for up to 5 years to compare the outcomes of HBV/HIV coinfection to HBV monoinfection.

A total of 149 HBV-infected patients were enrolled; 77 were coinfected with HIV. At baseline, HIV coinfection was associated with a higher HBV viral load (P < 0.0001) and higher platelet counts (P = 0.002). HIV coinfection was significantly associated with a higher risk of developing HCC after adjusting for age and sex (aHR 8.2; 95% CI 1.8–36.5; P = 0.006). The 5-year HCC incidence was 3.8% in HIV coinfected patients and 1.3% in HBV monoinfected patients (P = 0.2). The 5-year all-cause mortality was 8% in HIV coinfected patients and 3% in HBV monoinfected patients (P = 0.02). In a multivariate analysis, HIV coinfection was independently associated with an increased risk of death (aHR 2.5; 95% CI 1.3–4.8).

In this large South African cohort, HIV coinfection was independently associated with a higher risk of developing HCC and with a higher risk of death. These findings suggest that HBV/HIV coinfected patients have worse outcomes compared to HBV monoinfected patients, possibly related to a more advanced fibrosís in coinfected patients.

The objectives of this study were to explore the prevalence of psychiatric morbidity, substance use disorders and self-harm in a CHB cohort in sub-Saharan Africa and to describe the demographic and clinical characteristics of CHB patients with a history of psychiatric illness, substance use disorders and self-harm. In this cross-sectional study, we included adult patients (aged ≥ 18 years) with chronic hepatitis B infection, attending the outpatient clinic at the University of Cape Town, South Africa. Patients were recruited between January 2018 and December 2019. The Hospital Anxiety and Depression (HAD) scale, the 12-item General Health Questionnaire (GHQ-12), the Substance Use Disorder Screening Inventory (SUDSI), and an adapted version of the Questionnaire for Self-Injurious Thoughts and Behaviours (Q-STRiB) were used to screen for psychiatric morbidity, substance use disorders and self-harm. The χ2 test, t-test and Mann–Whitney U test were used to determine the differences between groups for categorical, normally distributed and non-normally distributed variables, respectively. A p-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. One hundred and fifteen patients with CHB were included in this study. The prevalence of probable anxiety disorder was 59% and that of probable depression was 41%. A third (34%) of the participants reported thinking about self-harm and 9% reported engaging in self-harm. Participants with a history of self-harm and psychiatric illness had significantly higher scores on the HAD and GHQ-12 than those without. Our results suggest that psychiatric morbidity and self-harm are common in people living with CHB in a middle-income country. This highlights the importance of screening for psychological co-morbidities in CHB programs.

English:

Researchers from the University of Liverpool have published a review of the evidence to give guidelines to clinicians in Africa on how to improve the treatment of hepatitis B.

Hepatitis B is a liver disease which affects 257 million people worldwide and causes 887,000 deaths each year. It is transmitted through blood exposure and the global infection burden is highest in East Asia, where the infection is mainly transmitted at the time of birth or during childhood. In Africa, the route of transmission is mainly sexual or through injection drug use, with an estimated global prevalence of 3.2% (95% UI 2.4-4.1). Unlike in East Asia, the infection in Africa is largely undiagnosed and therefore not treated, despite treatment being available.

Hepatitis B treatment can effectively prevent cirrhosis and liver cancer, but treatment guidelines recommend that therapy should only be started in people with advanced fibrosis. However, clinicians in Africa do not always have access to fibrosis assessment, so treatment could be improved if other, more accessible, strategies were used to guide treatment decisions.

In a new study, published today in the Journal of Hepatology, researchers from the Liverpool Infectious Diseases Institute at the University of Liverpool have reviewed the evidence to assess the effectiveness and practicality of different strategies to predict fibrosis in people with hepatitis B, and give guidelines to clinicians in Africa on how to improve the treatment of hepatitis B.

The studies reviewed provided evidence that a combination of simple, widely available tests could predict fibrosis in people with hepatitis B. The prediction tools require a blood test to measure the level of alanine transaminase (ALT), the liver’s activity; an ultrasound scan of the liver; and a test for hepatitis B infection, including knowledge of when the infection was acquired. Based on the results, clinicians can then decide whether to start treatment.

The researchers say that if the predicted fibrosis is low, then treatment is not required and can be delayed. If predicted fibrosis is high, then treatment can be started immediately. If the predicted fibrosis is in an intermediate range, then treatment can be delayed, which could help to improve the accessibility of treatment by extending the treatment window. If and when fibrosis assessment becomes available in clinical practice, then treatment can be initiated according to the results of the fibrosis assessment.

In the study, the researchers note that the mouse model they used mimics aspects of both acute and chronic HBV infection in humans. The researchers point out that the model does not incorporate all aspects of human disease, but captures some of the challenges involved in treating HBV infection. Acute HBV infection in humans is typically followed by the emergence of hepatitis B surface antibodies (anti-HBs), which provide protection against future HBV re-infection.

In the mouse model, the researchers were able to mimic this immune response using anti-HBs antibodies. The researchers point out that future studies will need to confirm if a similar immune response occurs in humans infected with both HBV and HIV.

The researchers also note that while both HBV and HIV are able to escape or evade the immune response, the combination of the two viruses may be less able to evade a response than HBV alone. The researchers indicate that further studies are needed to determine whether the same is true in humans.

The ECHO-HBV study is an open-label, randomised, controlled phase 2 trial of the safety and efficacy of 10 mg daily peg-IFN alfa-2a (Pegasys; Merck), given for 48 weeks. The primary outcome was sustained clearance of HBsAg for at least 9 months after the last dose of peg-IFN alfa-2a. The study enrolled 115 patients at 10 sites in South Africa and Zimbabwe between February, 2006, and May, 2007. All patients were HIV-1 infected and had HBV infection with HBeAg positivity and serum HBV DNA concentrations of at least 10 000 copies/mL. All patients were receiving antiretroviral therapy, and 84 (73%) were on highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART). Patients were randomly assigned to receive peg-IFN alfa-2a either alone or in combination with tenofovir (TDF; Viread, Bristol-Myers-Squibb) and emtricitabine (FTC; Emtriva, Gilead). The primary analysis was done on an intention-to-treat basis, and a per-protocol analysis was also done.

This study was done in collaboration with the University of KwaZulu-Natal, Durban, South Africa, and the University of Zimbabwe. The study was sponsored by Merck. The trial was registered under clinicaltrials.gov number NCT00337693.

Venn diagrams are named after John Venn, a British logician and philosopher who introduced the concept in 1881. The diagrams consist of overlapping circles, each representing a set of items. The overlapping region of the circles represents the items that are in common between the two sets. The region inside a single circle represents the items that are unique to that set. And the areas outside the circles represent the items that are unique to other sets.

Venn diagrams are versatile tools that can be used to solve a variety of problems. The purpose of this study was to examine the effects of a restorative justice intervention on reoffending among a sample of male offenders in Rwanda. Previous research has suggested that restorative justice interventions can reduce reoffending among participants compared to other justice interventions (i.e., incarceration) (e.g., [1, 2]). A restorative justice intervention provides an alternative to the traditional justice system by bringing together offenders, victims, and community members to discuss the harm caused by the offense and to work together to resolve the conflict and hold offenders accountable for their behavior [1, 3]. Several theoretical frameworks have been used to explain the effects of a restorative justice intervention on reoffending. Social learning theory [4] provides one such explanation. Social learning theory suggests that people learn through observation and reinforcement of behavior. An restorative justice intervention provides an opportunity for participants to learn pro-social behaviors through observing and practicing communication skills, empathy, and taking responsibility for one’s actions. Additionally, social learning theory suggests that restorative justice interventions expose participants to a range of consequences for their behavior which may reinforce pro-social behaviors (e.g., taking responsibility for one’s actions) and reduce the likelihood of antisocial behavior (i.e., reoffending) in the future.

English: The study aims to examine the impact of insecurity on women's entrepreneurial activities in Shiroro local government area of Niger State. The research questions that motivated this study are as follows: what are the causes and effect of insecurity on women's entrepreneurial activities in Shiroro local government area of Niger State? What are the challenges women are facing as a result of insecurity in their daily entrepreneurial activities in Shiroro local government area of Niger State? And what are the strategies women are using to survive their daily entrepreneurial activities in Shiroro local government area of Niger State? To achieve these objectives, a survey research design was used. The population of the study comprises all women entrepreneurs in Shiroro local government area of Niger State. The sample space was drawn from the population of women entrepreneurs in Shiroro local government area of Niger State. The sample size of the study was 100, which was drawn through a simple random sampling technique. Questionnaire was used as the instrument for data collection. Questionnaire was validated through the face and content validity. To ensure reliability of the instrument, the test-retest reliability was used. The data collected were analyzed using tables and frequency counts. From the findings, it was revealed that insecurity has caused great fear among women entrepreneurs and has led to the destruction of business properties. It was also revealed that women are not free to go about their daily business activities as it used to be before the coming in of insecurity. It was further revealed that women are now facing the challenges of insecurity in their daily entrepreneurial activities. The challenges include, destruction of business properties, loss of capital, fear of going out to buy goods for business, fear of going to the bank to take out loan for business, fear of travelling out to look for goods for business, and fear of employing workers. It was also revealed that women are using strategies to survive their daily entrepreneurial activities. The strategies include, selling of business properties and relocating to a less insecure place. From the findings, it was recommended that government should provide security in all the local government areas of Niger State. And women should be encouraged to form cooperative societies to enable them carry out their daily entrepreneurial activities without any fear. It was also recommended that government should provide jobs for the teeming unemployed youths in the local government areas of Niger State. This is because most of the times, the youths are the ones that take advantage of the situation to extort money from the women entrepreneurs.

Abstract: Background The risk of spontaneous preterm birth is increased in developing countries compared to developed countries. Maternal nutritional status may play an important role in the etiology of preterm birth. Methods We conducted a case-control study and measured maternal serum concentrations of selenium (Se), copper (Cu) and zinc (Zn) in early and late pregnancy in women from Malawi, South Africa and Tanzania. The outcome was spontaneous preterm birth. The cases were women delivering a live baby with birth weight less than 2500 g at 37 weeks gestation or less. Three controls per case, matched for age, parity and area of residence were selected. The serum concentrations of Se, Cu and Zn were measured with atomic absorption spectroscopy. Results The 157 sets of data (29 cases and 128 controls) showed that low maternal serum concentrations of Cu and Zn in early pregnancy and low maternal serum concentration of Se in late pregnancy were associated with an increased risk of spontaneous preterm birth. The risk of preterm birth increased with decreasing serum concentration of Cu and Zn in early pregnancy in quartiles (odds ratio 1.8, 95% confidence interval 1.0–3.1 and odds ratio 2.1, 95% confidence interval 1.2–3.5, respectively). The risk of preterm birth in the upper quartile compared to the lower quartile was 95% for Cu and 58% for Zn. The risk of preterm birth in women in the upper quartile was 3.2 compared to those in the lower quartile. The serum concentration of Se in late pregnancy was inversely associated with the risk of preterm birth. The risk of preterm birth in the upper compared to the lower decile was 4.0. Conclusions Low serum concentrations of Cu and Zn in early pregnancy and low serum concentration of Se in late pregnancy are associated with an increased risk of spontaneous preterm birth. Background

Preterm birth (PTB) is a leading cause of infant mortality and adverse long-term outcomes, including childhood growth restrictions and neurodevelopmental impairments. Dietary intake and nutritional status have been proposed as modifiable risk factors for preterm birth. However, the results of previous systematic reviews and meta-analyses of observational studies and randomized controlled trials evaluating the associations of zinc, copper, and selenium with PTB have been limited due to missing individual participant data.

Objectives

To evaluate the associations of zinc, copper, and selenium with PTB or PTB-associated adverse outcomes by conducting a systematic review and meta-analysis of available observational studies using individual participant data.

In this study, the researchers used data from the E3N-EPIC study, a cohort study conducted in France. During that period, the researchers analyzed the women’s blood samples for selenium, copper, and zinc concentrations.

The researchers found that women who had a history of preterm birth had higher concentrations of selenium, copper, and zinc than women who had never had a preterm birth. The risk of having a preterm birth decreased as the concentration of selenium increased. For example, for every 50 microgram per liter increase in selenium concentration, the risk of having a preterm birth decreased by 18%. The researchers also found that vitamin D and calcium concentrations in the blood did not differ between the two groups, but the women who had a history of preterm birth had higher concentrations of iron.

Dr. Turan added: “Our results suggest that high selenium concentration in blood may have a protective effect against preterm birth. Although the biological mechanism behind this is not known, selenium is an essential micronutrient that plays an important role in the immune system and in early development. Premature babies are also at increased risk of chronic childhood diseases such as asthma, diabetes, and autism. In addition, preterm birth is associated with long-term health problems for the mother, including heart disease, depression, and problems with subsequent pregnancies. The economic impact of preterm births is also significant, with an estimated annual cost in the United States of approximately $26 billion.

The risk of preterm birth can be reduced through a variety of strategies, including measures to promote healthy life-styles (e.g. weight control, smoking cessation) and measures to ensure the health of the mother and baby. Drugs that delay preterm labor are another important approach that has the potential to reduce the rate of preterm birth by more than one-third. Unfortunately, the most widely used drug for this purpose, misoprostol, does not appear to be effective when used alone and can actually increase the risk of preterm birth in some cases. Moreover, the use of misoprostol for this indication has been associated with serious side effects (including severe bleeding) and death. Therefore, there is an urgent need to identify new drugs that can safely and effectively delay preterm labor.

The overall goal of this project is to develop a novel small-molecule library that can be used to identify new drug leads for the delay of preterm birth. To achieve this, we will first use our validated in vitro and in vivo preterm birth models to screen a large, diverse library of approved pharmaceutical drugs (that are known to be safe in pregnancy) to identify those that are effective in delaying preterm birth. We will then use our established biochemical and cell biological tools to gain insight into the mechanisms by which the successful leads act to prolong pregnancy. This knowledge can then be used to design and synthesize analogs of the leads with improved activity and drug-like properties. The resulting optimized library will be screened in our preterm birth models to identify the most active compounds, which will then be tested in an in vivo model of preterm labor and birth. The project will generate novel scientific knowledge with practical applications that have the potential for a major impact on the health of pregnant women and their babies.

Dr. Paul English, from the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine said, “Given the high level of premature birth in Africa, and the low cost of the intervention, these are very exciting results. If confirmed in a trial, the impact could be huge.”

samples.ref: Halayen Gida da Amincewar Wuri da Yankunan Kunkuru mai faɗin baya (Malacochersus tornieri) a ƙasar Kenya
samples.hyp:
Pancake tortoise (Malacochersus tornieri) in Kenya

The Pancake tortoise (Malacochersus tornieri) is the second most popular tortoise in the pet trade after the red-footed tortoise (Geochelone carbonaria). Like other tortoises, they are long-lived, slow maturing, and relatively easy to keep. Unfortunately, this also makes them popular objects of international trade, and they are now threatened with extinction in the wild. In order to conserve wild populations, it is important to understand the basic natural history and behaviour of the species, and this information is key to developing appropriate conservation strategies. Radio telemetry was used to study the homing ability and site fidelity of tortoises in two study sites in Kenya, and the results indicate that they are able to home over long distances, and show high site fidelity. This is the first time that homing ability has been demonstrated in a tortoise. The high site fidelity of the Pancake tortoise has important implications for the conservation of this species, and suggests that habitat loss is of greater concern than predation or poaching as a threat to wild populations. The results also have important implications for the legal trade in Pancake tortoises, and may help to explain the high proportion of captive tortoises found in the pet trade that are claimed to be ‘wild’ or ‘free-living’.

Here we use data on the diet of a threatened canid species, the African wild dog Lycaon pictus, to examine if there are differences in the diet of dogs from two protected areas that vary in their antipredatory protection against hunting and if the diet of the dogs is a good indicator of the availability of prey. The African wild dog is a specialist predator that requires medium-sized to large prey, which are typically found in low densities in African savannas. Consequently, the importance of anthropogenic sources of food and prey items of carcases for wild dogs is debated. We used fecal analysis to determine the diet of wild dogs from two protected areas in Mozambique. We also investigated if dogs avoid areas where humans have been or hunted. We found that dogs from the Gorongosa National Park, which is actively protecting its boundaries, had a significantly lower consumption of anthropogenic prey and more wild prey compared to dogs from the Limpopo National Park, where protection against hunting pressure is limited to its national park boundaries. The results suggest that the diet of the wild dogs from Gorongosa reflects the availability of prey in the park, while the diet of the Limpopo dogs may be affected by illegal hunting and baiting outside of the national park, where large game is more abundant. This study highlights the importance of protected areas for conserving threatened carnivores and shows that the effectiveness of protected areas in conserving carnivores is dependent on the protection level around the national parks, highlighting the need for better managed buffer zones around protected areas.

The animals were found to occupy a mean (SD) home range of 39.2 (SD = 22.2) ha and a 95% spatial usage area of 124.1 (SD = 66.6) ha. samples.src: Lost pancake tortoises have an uncanny ability to ‘find home’
samples.ref: Kunkuru masu faɗin baya da suka ɓace suna da ikon mai ban mamaka na 'neman gida'
samples.hyp:
The study, led by the University of Bristol and the Aspinall Foundation, used satellite and ground tracking devices to show that the tortoises were able to navigate over 30km in the right direction to return to their home range.

This was true regardless of whether they were moving across flat landscapes or over more complex terrain.

Pancake tortoises are only found in the dry, rocky areas of south-western Madagascar, and are classified as Endangered by the IUCN Red List.

The main threat to their survival is habitat loss, but it is thought that large numbers are removed from the wild for the international wildlife trade.

Previous studies have shown that young individuals are particularly vulnerable to being captured and stolen, as they are sought after as pets and food source.

In this new study, published today in the journal Remote Sensing in Ecology and Conservation, the team tracked 15 pancake tortoises in south-west Madagascar over the course of one year.

They found that, by combining satellite and ground tracking data, they could distinguish between individuals and identify their home range – an area in which they spend most of their time for essential activities such as foraging and mating.

Co-investigator Dr Marine Julliard, from the University of Bristol’s School of Biological Sciences, said: “We were amazed to find that, even when displaced more than 3km away from their home range, these tortoises were able to return to their usual feeding grounds weeks later.

“We know they rely on visual cues to help them navigate back to their burrows, but it was surprising to see that they were able to navigate over such complex terrain, which included steep mountains, rivers and settlements.”

Co-investigator Dr Pascale de Lamothe, from the Aspinall Foundation, added: “The pancake tortoise has evolved extraordinary adaptations to survive in its harsh environment.

This new capability to ‘find home’ will be a valuable tool to help us protect this species from the threats of poaching and habitat loss.”

Senior Lecturer in the School of Biological Sciences at the University of Bristol, Professor Duncan Wullschleger, said: “This new method of tracking tortoises by combining satellite and ground data is highly accurate and will enable us to better protect these animals.

“We hope our findings will help inform conservation efforts to help this unique species survive, not only in Madagascar, but also in the wild in other parts of their range in Africa.”

The East African pancake tortoise is a small tortoise species that lives in arid and semi-arid areas of East Africa. The shell of the male animals is yellow with dark brown blotches, while the shell of the female animals is brown with seven distinctive yellow spots.

It also has important implications for the conservation of these animals, including those on the brink of extinction.

Tortoises are known to return to their birthplace, a behaviour known as ‘imprinting’, but it is not clear how they find their way over long distances. Some scientists think they may use the position of certain stars or the position of the Earth in relation to the Sun, but this has not been tested.

Our study tested whether the ability to find a home burrow after being translocated is affected by changes to the star map or the position of the Earth in relation to the Sun.

We translocated 14 tortoises over 160 km to an area with a different star map and different position of the Earth in relation to the Sun. We then tested how well they were able to home compared with 14 control animals that were not moved.

We found that the ability to home was not affected by changes to the star map or the position of the Earth in relation to the Sun. All the tortoises that were translocated returned directly to their home burrow without any errors, and most did so within 24 hours.

Homing is a remarkable ability that many animals possess. For example, birds can return to their birthplace despite being raised in an artificial environment with no view of the outside sky. The mechanism that birds use to do this is known as ‘homing pigeon navigation’.

The mechanism that tortoises use has been less clear, but this study advances our understanding and highlights the importance of further research in this area.

We investigated if lower doses given by intramuscular route could achieve serum concentrations similar to those achieved by intravenous therapy.

We enrolled children with culture-confirmed tuberculous meningitis. We assigned them to receive intramuscular rifampicin at 10 mg/kg twice weekly, or intravenous rifampicin at 20 mg/kg daily for 2 weeks. Serum rifampicin concentrations were measured by microbiological assay. The primary outcome was the attainment of rifampicin concentrations greater than 8 mg/L by day 10. The secondary outcomes were safety and tolerability, treatment cure rate, and death or neurologic sequelae at 6 months.

30 children were enrolled. Among 15 children who received intramuscular rifampicin, 14 (93%) attained rifampicin concentrations greater than 8 mg/L by day 10. Among 15 children who received intravenous rifampicin, 12 (80%) attained concentrations greater than 8 mg/L by day 10 (p = 0.496). One child in the intramuscular group had an acute anaphylactic reaction. The cure rates were 73% and 100% in the intramuscular and intravenous groups, respectively (p = 0.165). There were two deaths in the intramuscular group versus none in the intravenous group.

In children with culture-confirmed tuberculous meningitis, intramuscular rifampicin at a dose of 10 mg/kg twice weekly generated rifampicin serum concentrations similar to those achieved by intravenous therapy. This novel route of administration is suitable for resource-constrained settings.

The study was a collaboration between researchers from the University of Liverpool, the University of Cape Town, the South African Medical Research Council (SAMRC) and the Liverpool School of Tropical Medicine (LSTM).
Tuberculous meningitis is a serious form of tuberculosis (TB) that affects the meninges, the protective membranes that line the brain and spinal cord. It is a life-threatening disease with high mortality rates if left untreated. Standard treatment for tuberculous meningitis is a lengthy and complex course of multiple antibiotics that must be taken for many months. This makes it difficult for children, particularly those with the disease, to complete their treatment course. Failure to complete the course of treatment is one of the main reasons for treatment failure and the development of drug resistance. As a result, there is a critical need to develop new treatments that are simple, safe, and easy for children to follow.
Rifampicin is a standard first-line drug for the treatment of adult pulmonary TB and is a critical component of the treatment of tuberculous meningitis in children. However, it must be taken every 12 hours, making adherence to treatment a challenge. Oral administration of rifampicin every 24 hours has been shown to be comparable with dosing every 12 hours in terms of safety, side-effect profile, and efficacy for the treatment of pulmonary TB in adults. The same dosing regimen has also been shown to be non-inferior for the treatment of meningitis in a small study in Malawi, although the study was too small to detect any adverse events associated with the dosing regimen.
In this study, published in The Lancet Global Health, the team of researchers used an novel statistical model to assess the safety and efficacy of 24-hour dosing of rifampicin in children with tuberculous meningitis. The analysis included data from all available published and unpublished clinical trials of multidrug therapy for the treatment of childhood tuberculous meningitis, which included 198 children treated with rifampicin given as a 12-hourly injection or tablet and 87 children treated with rifampicin given as a 24-hourly tablet.
The use of the novel statistical model allowed the researchers to include data from all available studies without the need to wait for the publication or completion of ongoing trials. MTB is associated with a higher mortality than pulmonary tuberculosis and the addition of HIV to the equation increases the risk of death even further.

Rifampicin is known to be active against both tuberculosis and HIV, and in laboratory studies it has shown synergy with antiretroviral drugs, which enhance their activity against HIV. High-dose rifampicin is the same dose used to treat tuberculosis, but administered once a day rather than twice a day. The review found that treatment success was significantly higher in patients treated with high-dose rifampicin (64%) than in those treated with standard dose rifampicin (34%). High-dose rifampicin was particularly effective in patients who were not responding to treatment with standard dose rifampicin.

Although high-dose rifampicin was able to improve outcomes in these patients, the researchers note that the study was limited by the heterogeneity of the patient population and the non-randomized study design. They therefore call for a randomized controlled trial of high-dose rifampicin in HIV-positive patients with MTB.

This study shows that the same is true for the brain itself. The study was small, but it does raise some important questions about how to improve treatment for TB meningitis.

The study enrolled 11 patients with both tuberculosis meningitis and HIV. All of the patients were treated with standard three-drug therapy for TB, which includes rifampicin. Because HIV also weakens the immune system, these patients were also treated with anti-HIV drugs. After two weeks, all of the patients were treated with intrathecal (into the spinal fluid) injections of rifampicin. The researchers were able to collect cerebrospinal fluid and brain tissue samples from four of the patients who died.

The study showed that, after two weeks of treatment, the concentration of rifampicin in the cerebrospinal fluid was still only one quarter to one half of the optimal concentration. In three of the four brains examined, no rifampicin was detected. And even in the one brain where some rifampicin was found, the concentration was too low to be effective.

This study confirms the need for new drugs or new delivery systems for tuberculosis meningitis, the researchers say. The problem with rifampicin across the blood-brain barrier is similar to the problem with another TB drug, isoniazid. Several new TB drugs are under development, some of which are in the final testing stages. If these drugs prove to be safe and effective, they would probably be used in combination with older drugs like rifampicin and isoniazid.

Rifampicin is a cornerstone of TB treatment because it is taken up so well by the bacteria that it can clear an infection in just two months, while other drugs have to be taken for six months. If doctors could get rifampicin into the brain in higher concentrations, it might be possible to shorten the duration of TB treatment, which would be a big advantage because TB is a difficult disease to treat for such a long time.

The aim of the study was to find out if a higher dose of rifampicin is safe and how well it works in children and adolescents living in resource-limited settings.
Rifampicin is one of the first-line drugs used to treat tuberculosis and is part of the basic treatment regimen, which also includes isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol. These drugs are effective against all forms of bacteria that cause tuberculosis. Rifampicin is also used in the treatment of mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) and in the prevention and treatment of tuberculosis in people with HIV.
Tuberculosis meningitis is a severe form of tuberculosis that affects the membranes that surround the brain and spinal cord. It is the most common cause of adult and childhood bacterial meningitis. Each year, an estimated 40,000 people develop this form of tuberculosis, and it is the most frequent cause of death from tuberculosis in children in many parts of the world. It is also one of the most frequent causes of death from tuberculosis in people with HIV.
The study included 244 children and adolescents with culture-confirmed tuberculosis meningitis. The patients were treated with rifampicin at standard doses (10 mg/kg) or higher doses (15 mg/kg). The study showed that increasing the dose of rifampicin by 5 mg/kg per day was safe and that patients given higher doses of rifampicin were 69% less likely to die or develop neurological deficits.
The study was conducted in three sites in Côte d’Ivoire and one site in Mali. The sites are located in Abidjan, Bouaké, Korhogo, and Bamako. The study was conducted by an international research group, the Pediatric Tuberculosis Clinical Trials Consortium (PCTCC), and involved 12 collaborating institutions from the United States, Africa, Asia, and South America. The study was funded by the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases and the Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development, both part of the National Institutes of Health.

The study is enrolling patients at sites in Botswana, Haiti, South Africa, Thailand, Uganda, and the United States. All the patients are treated for tuberculosis as per national guidelines. Half of the patients are randomly assigned to take high-dose rifampicin and the other half to take standard-dose rifampicin. The plan is to enroll 400 patients. The study is sponsored by the HIV Pathogenesis CO-Morbidities and Complications (HPCCC) Consortium. Michael Harrison, director of the Center for AIDS Research at the University of California, San Francisco, is the study chair.

The study is divided into two parts. In the first part, the researchers are assessing the safety of high-dose rifampicin. If the safety data show that high-dose rifampicin is not over-tolerated, the researchers will continue with the second part of the study. In the second part, the researchers will compare the effects of high-dose and standard-dose rifampicin on the severity of the HIV disease. The primary outcome of the study is the change in the level of HIV RNA in the blood after one year of treatment.

The study is being conducted as a randomized, open-label trial. Patients are randomly assigned to take either high-dose or standard-dose rifampicin. The study has a 2:1 ratio. This means that for every two patients assigned to take standard-dose rifampicin, one patient is assigned to take high-dose rifampicin. The assignment is done by a computer. The patients and the research team are informed about the dose group to which each patient is assigned, but the assignment is not disclosed to the patients.

The duration of the study is approximately two years and nine months. The patients are followed for the duration of the study.

The patients in the study are adults with HIV and tuberculosis meningitis. To be eligible for the study, the patients must be between the ages of 15 and 65 and have a CD4 cell count of 100 or less. samples.hyp:
In this study, we investigated the extent of soil fertility decline in smallholder farming systems in Ethiopia, Kenya, Malawi, Tanzania, and Uganda, and assessed the role of management in the decline. We used long-term (30–40 years) farm survey data from 48 farms in the study countries. We calculated the change in the production of six soil fertility indicators (mineral nutrient status, soil organic carbon, soil microbial biomass, soil nitrogen mineralization, soil quality, and crop yield) over time at each farm and related these changes to changes in management (e.g., changes in the application of crop residue, inorganic fertilizer, and nutrient- and water-conserving practices such as conservation tillage, mulching, and irrigation). We found large differences in the extent and rate of soil fertility decline among the study countries. In Uganda and Malawi, soil fertility declined moderately over the study period (1971–2009/10) across all soil fertility indicators, but the decline was small or even reversed in some of the other countries. The rate of soil fertility decline was more rapid where there was a greater reliance on maize as a cash crop and a lower reliance on nutrient-conserving practices such as mulching and tree cover. The use of inorganic fertilizer was not a major driver of soil fertility decline, but it was an important enabler of yield growth where it was used. We conclude that soil fertility management in smallholder farming systems should focus on increasing the use of nutrient-conserving practices and improving the efficiency of inorganic fertilizer use. Our results provide guidance for policies and investments designed to enhance the sustainability of crop production in sub-Saharan Africa.

However, the effect of combined application of biochar and compost on soil fertility and maize (Zea mays L.) production has received little attention.

The objective of this study was to evaluate the effect of combined application of biochar and compost on soil fertility and maize production. A laboratory incubation experiment was conducted in the laboratory of the Soil Science Department, University of Wisconsin-Madison, USA, and a field experiment was conducted in the research farm of the University of Wisconsin-Madison, USA, and the International Maize and Wheat Improvement Center (CIMMYT), El Batan, Egypt. The laboratory incubation experiment was conducted using a completely randomized design with four replications. The treatments were no biochar and no compost (control), biochar alone, compost alone, and the combination of biochar and compost. The field experiment was conducted using a randomized complete block design with four replications. The treatments were no biochar and no compost (control), biochar alone (15 t ha−1), compost alone (25 t ha−1), and the combination of biochar and compost (15 and 25 t ha−1, respectively). In the laboratory experiment, soil microbial biomass was significantly higher in the combination of biochar and compost treatment than in the other treatments. The combination of biochar and compost treatment had higher basal respiration and substrate induced respiration compared to the other treatments, indicating higher microbial activity and substrate utilization, respectively. The combination of biochar and compost treatment had higher amounts of mineralizable N than the other treatments. The combination of biochar and compost increased grain yield, biomass yield, and nitrogen uptake by 79, 78, and 67 g m−2, respectively, compared to the control in the field experiment. The interactive effect of biochar and compost on maize plant height was not significant. However, there was a significant interaction between biochar and compost on maize leaf chlorophyll content where the combination of biochar and compost had higher leaf chlorophyll content than the other treatments. The combination of biochar and compost treatment had higher amounts of available P and exchangeable Ca than the other treatments. The combination of biochar and compost increased soil cation exchange capacity (CEC), available P, and exchangeable Ca compared to biochar and compost alone. The combination of biochar and compost is the most effective treatment for improving soil health and maize yield.

The results of this study showed that the combination of biochar and compost has a positive effect on soil properties and maize yield.

samples.ref: Wannan binciken ya binciki yadda za a iya amfani da gawayi, wani abu mai qarko, mai yawan sinadarin kabon da aka yi daga sinadarin bayomas, da aka jefar, don inganta yanayin ƙasa a yankin Saharar Afirka.
samples.hyp:
Biochar has been shown to improve plant growth through changes in soil chemistry, physics and microbiology. However, little is known about the mechanisms driving these effects, limiting biochar use in the region. We incubated biochar with 20 soils representing five countries in sub-Saharan Africa and quantified changes in soil nitrogen dynamics to determine how biochar affects soil fertility. Biochar had both positive and negative effects on soil nitrogen dynamics. It increased microbial nitrogen transformation rates, decreased mineralization inhibition, and minimized the negative impact of alum on nitrogen cycling, indicating that biochar can reduce alum toxicity to soil microbes. Biochar interactions with soils were highly dependent on the C:N of the biochar feedstock used. Biochar made from a high-C:N feedstock (rice straw) had the greatest impact on microbial nitrogen transformation rates and mineralization, while biochar made from low-C:N feedstock (sunflower meal) had the greatest impact on nitrification. Our results indicate that the quality of biochar feedstocks and their interactions with soils have the potential to significantly influence the efficacy of biochar as a soil amendment.

Biochar; Sub-Saharan Africa; nitrogen; soil fertility; rice straw; alum; sunflower meal

Biochar is produced by heating plant material in an oxygen-free environment. This produces a charcoal-like material with an electrical conductivity close to that of soil.

In a recent study published in the Journal of Environmental Management, researchers evaluated the effect of biochar and soil inoculation with bacteria from surface crop residues on plant growth in an agricultural soil.

The study was conducted in Brazil, where farmers typically burn crop residues after the harvest. This practice has both positive and negative effects on soil. Ash from the burning of crop residue increases soil pH and provides nutrients to plants. However, it can also reduce the amount of organic matter in soil, which can have a negative impact on plant growth.

In the study, researchers added biochar to soil from an agricultural region in Brazil to determine whether it could improve plant growth. In addition to adding biochar to part of the soil, the researchers also added bacteria from surface crop residues to another part of the soil. The bacteria were collected from the surface of a corn crop and added to the soil at a rate of 0.01% of the soil’s weight.

The researchers then planted sunflower seeds in the soil and collected them when they reached 70 days old. They found that adding both biochar and bacteria to the soil increased the number of sunflower plants that grew by 96%. It also increased the height of the sunflower plants by 25%.

The study shows that biochar and soil bacteria can work together to improve plant growth. However, it is important to note that not all bacteria are beneficial to plants. Some bacteria can actually harm plants. Therefore, it is important to use bacteria that are known to be beneficial to plants.

In conclusion, this study shows that biochar can be used to improve soil fertility and support plant growth. It is important for farmers to consider using biochar as a way to improve the health of their soil and increase the productivity of their crops.

samples.hyp:
We hypothesized that fibrin formed in the presence of citrullinated fibrinogen (CIT-fibrinogen) has altered biophysical properties, which can be “unmasked” by certain external factors. Such altered fibrin properties may predispose to thrombosis. The A2 domain of fibrin is critical for interactions with cells and thrombus formation. We tested the effect of CIT-fibrinogen on incorporation of fibrin into multimeric protein clusters on the surface of human platelets, and its impact on the platelet cytoskeleton and thrombus formation on the platelet surface in the presence of calcium ion (Ca2+) and adenosine diphosphate (ADP). We also characterized the effect of CIT-fibrinogen on fibrin structure and activation of the intracellular signaling protein p38 mitogen-activated protein kinase (p38 MAPK) in human platelets. Fibrin formed in the presence of CIT-fibrinogen was incorporated into the platelet surface in a Ca2+- and ADP-dependent manner. CIT-fibrinogen-dependent fibrin-platelet interactions were dependent on the activation of the glycoprotein GPIIb-IIIa (integrin αIIbβ3) and the associated intracellular signaling protein p38 MAPK. In addition, CIT-fibrinogen induced conformational changes in fibrin, which was reflected in the increased activation of p38 MAPK. Our results suggest that the altered biophysical properties of fibrin formed in the presence of CIT-fibrinogen, and CIT-fibrinogen-induced changes in the fibrin structure, target platelet GPIIb-IIIa and p38 MAPK and promote platelet fibrin(ogen) interactions and thrombus formation. These findings provide new mechanistic insights into the prothrombotic effects of autoantibodies against citrullinated fibrinogen.

This in vitro test analyzes the viscoelastic properties of the clot formed during coagulation.

A thromboelastograph curve is shown in Fig. 1. The parameters measured are the clotting time (CT, s), the amplitude of the amplitude ratio unit A (AUR, %) at 60 min, and the maximum lysis occurred at 60 min (ML%, %). Shown in Fig. 2 are the individual values of CT, AUR, and ML% for the 22 healthy subjects and 22 patients with early-stage breast cancer. Statistics were calculated using the Mann–Whitney U test. P values less than 0.05 were considered significant.

Published: Tuesday, May 19, 2009 - 12:00am

By: David J. Tenenbaum

BOSTON – The reason why arthritis patients have a higher risk of heart attack and stroke may be related to blood clotting, according to researchers at Boston University School of Medicine (BUSM) and Boston Medical Center (BMC).

The study, which appears online today in the journal Arthritis & Rheumatism, is the first to link blood clotting to cardiovascular disease in this patient population. It also suggests that anti-clotting drugs, such as aspirin and Plavix, could be beneficial in preventing cardiovascular events in patients with rheumatoid arthritis.

“While our study does not directly address the question of whether anti-clotting therapies could prevent cardiovascular disease in patients with rheumatoid arthritis, it does provide data suggesting that such therapies might be beneficial,” said corresponding author Michael C. Hochberg, MD, associate professor of medicine and director of the BU-BMC Rheumatology Program.

Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic, inflammatory disease that affects about 1 percent of the population. Patients with RA have a three-fold increased risk of heart attack and a two-fold increased risk of stroke compared to the general population. The reason for this remains unclear, however, because RA patients often have risk factors for heart disease such as high levels of cholesterol, diabetes, smoking and obesity. Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of decreased quality of life and increased mortality in RA patients.

Hochberg and his team had previously shown that RA patients have higher levels of two proteins D-dimer and soluble P-selectin (sP-selectin) than healthy individuals. Higher levels of these proteins are associated with an increased risk of cardiovascular disease because they are markers of blood clot formation. In the current study, the researchers set out to determine the relationship between these two proteins, inflammation and to see if these relationships were associated with cardiovascular events (heart attack and stroke).

The team, which included researchers from the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute, found that higher levels of sP-selectin were associated with increased levels of C-reactive protein (CRP), a marker of inflammation, in the RA patients. Increased levels of both sP-selectin and CRP were associated with a higher risk of cardiovascular events.

“Higher levels of sP-selectin and D-dimer in patients with RA may explain, in part, their increased risk of heart attack and stroke,” said Hochberg.

It is a systemic condition, affecting multiple organs, and not just the joints.

The underlying causes of rheumatoid arthritis are not fully understood, but it is an autoimmune condition where the body’s immune system, which normally fights infection, attacks the body’s own tissues. This leads to inflammation, which is a common feature of RA. The inflammation can affect many organs and tissues including the heart, eyes, lungs, and skin. The most specific feature of RA is inflammation of the synovial membrane that lines the joints. This membrane thickens, becomes inflamed, and produces an excessive amount of synovial fluid, which can cause damage to the joint and result in pain and stiffness. RA can also affect the lining of the heart and large blood vessels, causing inflammation in the heart (pericarditis) and inflammation of the aorta (aortitis). This can result in shortness of breath, palpitations, chest pain, and fatigue. The lungs may be affected, causing cough and tightness in the chest. RA can also affect the skin and eyes. In the skin, rheumatoid nodules are firm, painless lumps that may develop under the skin in areas with a lot of friction, such as the elbows, knees, or the heel of the hand. In the eyes, inflammation of the lining of the eye (iritis) or inflammation of the middle layer of the eye (epi-retina) can occur, which can cause pain in the eyes, redness, blurred vision, or even vision loss.

Rheumatoid arthritis is a chronic condition, meaning it lasts a long time. RA can be intermittent, with periods of flare-ups (flares) and remission (when there are no symptoms). The course of the disease can be unpredictable, with periods of relative inactivity (remission) and sudden exacerbations of disease activity (flare-ups). Early diagnosis and treatment is important to minimize joint damage.

samples.ref: A taqaice dai, masu binciken sun gwada illar kumburi da canjin tsarin protin da ke da alaqa da dunqulewar jini wanda ake kira fibrins.
samples.hyp:
They found that inflammation and structural changes induced a significant conformational change in fibrin structure, which in turn affected the ability of fibrin to bind to another protein called von Willebrand factor (vWF), which is essential for blood clotting.

This research is important because blood clots are a crucial part of the body's healing response, but excessive blood clotting can lead to life-threatening conditions such as deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, and stroke. Understanding how inflammation and structural changes affect fibrin and vWF interactions is essential for developing new treatments for these conditions.

The researchers used a combination of biochemistry, biophysics, and computational methods to examine the effects of inflammation and structural changes on fibrin and vWF interactions. They found that the inflammatory protein, interleukin-1beta (IL-1β), and a structural change called gamma polymerase-induced clots (γPS) both increased the amount of vWF required to form a blood clot. This is significant because it suggests that the body may need more vWF to counteract the effects of inflammation and structural changes on blood clotting.

In addition to examining the effects of inflammation and structural changes on fibrin and vWF interactions, this research also investigated the effects on another protein called plasminogen. Plasminogen is a protein that helps to break down blood clots, and understanding how inflammation and structural changes affect its interaction with fibrin and vWF is important for developing treatments that promote clot resolution without adverse effects.

Overall, this research provides valuable insights into the complex interactions between inflammation, structural changes, and blood clotting proteins. By revealing how these factors affect each other, this knowledge can inform the development of new treatments that are better tailored to individual patient needs and improve our understanding of the underlying mechanisms of blood clotting and resolution.

The researchers, including those from the University of Cambridge, found that by targeting a specific region of the fibrin protein, called the carboxy-terminal dabase (CTD), they were able to significantly slow-down or even prevent blood clotting in the damaged vessels. 

In the study, the researchers used a genetically encoded antibody fragment - known as a nanobody - to target the CTD of fibrin. This was able to access previously untargetable regions of fibrin, including those that are involved in initial clot formation and subsequent maturation. The team were then able to use this nanobody to develop a polymerase chain reaction (PCR) screening method to identify potential drug targets on the fibrin CTD. 

By screening the human fibrin CTD, the researchers were able to identify several previously uncharacterized regions that are exposed during clotting and therefore could serve as drug targets. 

The team then validated their screening method by treating human plasma with three different nanobodies, which all targeted the fibrin CTD. This treatment significantly reduced blood clotting in the damaged vessels. If further developed, this treatment may one day be used in individuals with conditions that are caused by blood clots, such as acute myocardial infarction (AMI), ischemic stroke and deep vein thrombosis (DVT). 

Professor Mandel said: “Blood clots are a complex structure, with many different proteins working together to form them. By targeting one of these key proteins, we were able to interfere with, and in some cases, even prevent blood clotting in damaged vessels. While this is just a proof of principle study, it does offer us several potential targets that we can develop further.” 

Dr. Lucia Gandoglia, from the University of Milano, added: “Prolonged clotting, as well as inappropriate dissolution, is associated with adverse clinical events. Therefore, the possibility of regulating the clotting process at the level of the fibrin CTD is of potential therapeutic value.” 

Dr. Julien Feron, from the University of Cambridge, said: “This study shows that by targeting the same region of the fibrin CTD with different nanobodies, we get different effects in terms of regulating blood clotting. This suggests there are many unexplored regions of the fibrin CTD, which could be potential targets for new anticoagulant drugs.”

This article is a direct response to a recent publication by van Heerden et al1 on the use of the same dataset to investigate the efficacy of the 2019 BCG vaccine on COVID-19 incidence in South Africa. Both studies used a similar method to investigate whether prior BCG vaccination modified COVID-19 incidence in South Africa. Our study3 used a case—control study of 5,888 COVID-19 confirmed cases and 20,741 controls matched for age, sex, race and area of residence to calculate odds ratios (OR) of COVID-19 disease for individuals who received the 1974 BCG vaccine compared to unvaccinated individuals. We found that prior exposure to the 1974 BCG vaccine was protective (OR = 0.63 95% CI 0.45–0.88, p = 0.006) against COVID-19 disease. This is in contrast to the study by van Heerden et al who used a case—survival study of 87,802 COVID-19 confirmed cases to investigate the impact of the 2019 BCG vaccination program on survival from COVID-19. The authors found that individuals who received the 2019 BCG vaccine had a 3.5-fold higher mortality risk than unvaccinated individuals (HR 3.58, 95% CI 2.78–4.59, p = 0.0001). samples.src: Marine meteorological forecasts for coastal ocean users – perceptions, usability and uptake
samples.ref: Hasashen yanayi na yanayin ruwa don masu amfani da bakin teku – fahimta, amfani da ɗauka
samples.hyp:
© 2023 International Journal of Biometeorology

The accuracy and lead time of marine meteorological forecasts are largely dependent on the underlying numerical weather prediction (NWP) model. The NWP model is run at a variety of horizontal spatial resolutions and the impact of this on the marine forecasts was analysed in this study. In addition, the perceptions of marine users on the usability of the forecasts were investigated. The study employed a web-based questionnaire survey, which was distributed to marine users. Data were collected on user characteristics, weather forecasting needs and perceptions on the marine forecasts provided by the UK Met Office. Results indicate that marine users have different forecasting requirements, depending on their coastal activities. The high seas forecasts, based on the coarse resolution Global Forecast System (GFS) model, were perceived to be the most useful for general inshore forecasting needs, in particular for wind and wave forecasts. The medium resolution (approx. 10 km) operational models, such as the ARPEGE, UKV and ECMWF models, were considered to be more appropriate for specific activities, e.g. for port operations or offshore oil and gas, and for areas with high topographical variability. There was a general preference for 2–4 day forecasts. The accuracy and usefulness of the wave height forecasts were considered to be the most important factors in marine meteorological forecasts, and there was a clear preference for the wave height forecasts over the significant wave height forecasts. The wind speed forecasts were considered to be less useful, and more variable than those for the significant wave height and direction. Marine users would prefer to have wave direction included in the official forecasts. The official marine forecasts were considered to be useful but not entirely satisfactory. The marine users indicated that the marine forecasts were not used to plan their activities, but rather to adapt their plans if the weather conditions turned out to be different from what was forecast. This suggests that the official forecasts are underutilised. Marine users would favor more user-friendly products, with a less technical style of writing, and more consistent forecasts. They would also favor products which provide a higher initial value and longer lead time, even if these have to be based on a coarser resolution model. It is concluded that the official marine forecasts are not fully optimized for marine users. There is a need to better meet the requirements of the marine user community, e.g. by developing more user-friendly products.
