samples.hyp: The usability gap refers to the difference between the amount of scientific information that is needed by the public to make informed decisions and the amount of information that is actually available to the public. The assumption is that the public does not have the knowledge or understanding of the science that is needed to make decisions about policy and technology. The usability gap has been a focus of information scientists for over 30 years. The goal of this research is to gain a better understanding of the usability gap in the context of biotechnology. The research questions are: 1) What is the usability gap for biotechnology? 2) How do different groups (e.g. gender, education) perceive the science and risk information related to biotechnology? 3) What is the public’s opinion on the type of information they need to make decisions about biotechnology? 4) What are the perceived barriers to understanding biotechnology? The theoretical framework for this research is based on the idea that the usability gap is created by differences in the knowledge and understanding of science between experts (i.e. scientists) and non-experts (i.e. the public). This research is innovative in that it uses a combination of methods to examine the usability of biotechnology information. It combines qualitative and quantitative data to provide a more complete picture of the science related knowledge and understanding of the public. It uses data from a survey administered to a sample of U.S. residents and data from a series of focus groups. Survey data will be analyzed using statistical techniques to examine differences in science knowledge and understanding related to biotechnology between different groups of respondents. Focus group data will be analyzed using a constant comparative method to identify themes that describe how respondents understand biotechnology and risk information related to biotechnology. The combination of these data will then be used to generate hypotheses about the usability gap for biotechnology. South Africa and Australia. The aim of this research is to develop an understanding of the importance of metocean information to coastal users in South Africa and Australia and to identify the information needs of these users. The research was conducted in two stages. In the first stage, a series of semi-structured interviews were conducted with coastal users in each country. The interviews were designed to investigate the types and formats of metocean information that users need. The second stage of the research was conducted by means of a survey. The survey was distributed to a range of coastal users in each country to determine the frequency and salience of metocean information needs. The survey was designed to identify the types of metocean information most frequently needed by users and to determine the situations in which these needs arise. The research identified a general need for metocean information among the coastal users that were surveyed. The most salient need was to avoid loss or damage to property as a result of coastal hazards. The next most salient need was to plan and execute activities such as swimming, surfing and boating. The research also identified several other important uses of metocean information. These include: maintaining safety and well-being; planning and executing projects; complying with regulations; and ensuring business continuity. The research provides new insights into the salience of metocean information for coastal users in Australia and South Africa. The research has identified several new aspects relating to the salience, types, formats and sources of metocean information that could be used to improve the provision of metocean information services for coastal users in Australia and South Africa. These findings have the potential to improve the provision of metocean information and services and to assist coastal managers in making better decisions that contribute to sustainable management of coastal environments.

samples.src: South Africans, New Zealanders trust forecasts about the weather at sea
samples.ref: ’Yan Afirka ta Kudu, ‘yan New Zealand sun amince da hasashen yanayi a teku
samples.hyp:
more than forecasts about the weather on land. This is one of the conclusions of a study conducted by Professor Dr. Jan Kummerow of the Institute of Psychology at the University of Bonn, Germany, and Professor Dr. Thomas Sutter of the University of Zurich, Switzerland. The study was published in the scientific journal PLOS ONE.

The researchers showed 1,000 South Africans and New Zealanders weather forecasts for land and sea. The forecasts were presented in a way that is common in the media: a weather map with symbols for air pressure, wind, cloud cover and temperature, accompanied by a brief text. The participants had to rate how confident they were in the forecasts on a scale from zero (not at all confident) to 100 (very confident).

The forecasts for the weather at sea were trusted more than the forecasts for the weather on land. On average, the participants gave 68 out of 100 points for the sea forecasts and 58 points for the land forecasts. The researchers also asked the participants how often they thought the weather forecasts were correct. Sea forecasts were rated as correct more often than land forecasts.

The participants in the study were not sailors or fishermen. "The study was conducted on a random sample of the general population," Kummerow explains. "The participants were not at all familiar with weather forecasts for sea. But they were presented with the same information as sailors get."

Why do the forecasts for the weather at sea seem more trustworthy? Kummerow: "One reason may be that the weather at sea is more extreme than the weather on land. The media often show spectacular images of violent storms at sea. This could lead to the assumption that it is easier to make correct forecasts for the weather at sea than for the weather on land."

Kummerow and Sutter also showed the participants weather forecasts for Germany and New Zealand. The results were the same: the forecasts for the weather at sea were trusted more than the forecasts for the weather on land.

The study was funded by the German Research Foundation (DFG) and the Swiss National Science Foundation (SNF). The authors would also like to thank the South African Weather Service for supporting the study.

samples.hyp: The first step is to identify the phenomenon that is causing the problem. In the case of the ozone, the problem was that certain human activities were releasing gases that, when combined with others, were destroying the ozone layer that protects the Earth from ultraviolet radiation. The second step is to identify what is causing the problem. In the case of the ozone, it was chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs), a group of human-made gases that were introduced in the 1920s as replacements for the natural gases that refrigerators and air conditioners use to expel heat. The third step is to identify what could replace the material that is causing the problem. Scientists identified the replacement for CFCs as hydrochlorofluorocarbons (HCFCs), a group of human-made gases that are destroyed more quickly in the atmosphere and do not deplete the ozone layer. The fourth step is to identify how to get rid of the material that is causing the problem. The answer was to replace the CFCs in refrigerants and air conditioners with HCFCs, which are not as harmful to the environment. The fifth step is to identify how to keep people from doing things that are causing the problem. The answer was to regulate the use of CFCs and to find alternative technologies that do not use CFCs. The sixth step is to identify how to stop new sources of the material that is causing the problem from being created. The answer was to stop manufacturing CFCs altogether. The seventh step is to identify how to clean up the mess that is left behind by the material that is causing the problem. The ozone layer is returning, and should be completely back to normal by 2050. The eighth step is to identify how to prevent the problem from ever happening again. This is where the Montreal Protocol goes beyond science and into politics. The key to preventing the depletion of the ozone layer was to ban the production of CFCs. Coastal citizens’ use of tropical cyclone forecasts in the Philippines
Copyright 2023 Science Press
The Philippines is the country in the world that is most frequently hit by tropical cyclones. The season starts in June and can cause heavy rain, storm surges and devastating winds. To alert the population in good time, a forecast is needed. But who uses these forecasts and for what purposes? An international team of researchers including Dr. Marco Dümenil from the University of Bern’s Oeschger Centre for Climate Change Research has now explored these questions in the Philippines. The scientists interviewed more than 1,300 people in the north of the country. They found that the forecasts are used mainly for planning activities, such as construction work. The forecasts are most frequently obtained from commercial media, but the government’s weather service also plays an important role. “The forecasts are most trusted if they are obtained from various sources and if the users themselves can check the forecast’s accuracy,” Dümenil explains. If the forecasts are used for daily activities, the citizens often rely on their own experience. The researchers suspect that this is because the forecasts are often too general to be of use for individual decisions. The authors recommend that the government should make available the raw data of the forecast models, and should train the population in how to use the forecasts. In this way, coastal citizens could make better use of the forecasts to protect their lives and property.

samples.src: A Participatory Approach to Assessing the Climate-Smartness of Agricultural Interventions:
samples.ref: Hanyar Haɗaka don Tantance Aikin Noma mai Jure Sauyin Yanayi:
samples.hyp:
Lessons from Goldilocks and the Three Bears

Wheat is a key crop for smallholder farmers in the highlands of East Africa, but productivity is severely constrained by drought. Precision agriculture offers the potential to increase water use efficiency, but requires significant management capacity—impractical for the smallholder context. Co-designing precision agriculture interventions with smallholders as an agent of change provides the opportunity to understand how these technologies can be climate-smart. This paper takes a participatory approach to assess the climate-smartness of precision nutrient management and weather-based agronomic insights on wheat in Uganda. Across four sites and 240 smallholders, we quantified the adoption and potential impacts of these interventions, including gender and age effects. We found that: (i) smallholders adopted the low-input precision approaches we studied (ii) there were substantial weather-related effects on nutrient recommendations and crop performance, and (iii) the impacts of the interventions were gendered, with positive effects for productivity and farm income for women, and negative effects for crop insurance for men. Co-design is a participatory approach that allows for an up-front assessment of the climate-smartness of interventions, and provides real-time adaptation based on on-farm results. This approach supports the identification of climate-smart interventions and enhances their adoption, increasing their potential impact.

Study: A Descriptive Epidemiological Study of Buruli Ulcer in Lushoto District, Tanzania

Buruli ulcer (BU) is a chronic, necrotic skin ulceration caused by the gram-positive bacterium Mycobacterium ulcerans.
The disease is endemic in some parts of sub-Saharan Africa, where the number of cases has increased in recent years.
This study aimed to determine the epidemiological features of BU in Lushoto district, Tanzania.
A descriptive epidemiological study of all patients with histologically confirmed BU in Lushoto district between January 2014 and December 2018 was conducted.
A case was defined as a human skin lesion consistent with BU, present for >2 weeks and confirmed by histopathology to be due to M. ulcerans.
A total of 127 cases were included in this study.
The mean age of the patients was 31 years (range 6–85 years), 63.4% were male.
Most of the cases occurred in the rainy season, March–May (59.1%).
The typical lesion appeared on the extremities, most commonly the arm (67.8%), especially the forearm (60.6%), followed by the leg (16.9%) and then the foot (14.6%).
The clinical diagnosis was confirmed by histopathology in all cases.
The majority of the patients (88.5%) had a positive tuberculin skin test.
20.3% of the patients had a comorbid comitant infection.
The most common co-infection was with Schistosoma spp. (14.2%).
BU occurred more frequently in patients with low levels of education, illiterates (38.6%) followed by those with primary school education (35.8%).
BU is an insidious disease that can easily be misdiagnosed.
The results of this study can help health officials to develop strategies for disease control.

Secondly, there is a lack of information on the cost-effectiveness of climate change interventions. Thirdly, there is a lack of climate change interventions that have been successfully implemented at scale. Finally, there is a lack of knowledge on how to upscale and outscale successful climate change interventions.

The main aim of this thesis was to contribute to the understanding of how climate change interventions can be made more effective, in order to achieve the highest possible impact. The specific aims were to identify and discuss 1) potential climate change impacts and 2) existing and proposed climate change interventions. Finally, the thesis aimed to identify and discuss 3) gaps in the climate change intervention landscape, as well as 4) possible solutions to addressing these gaps. The thesis did this by conducting a systematic review of literature, and by conducting seven interviews with key informants from the Mozambique context.

The results of the literature review indicate that there is a need to 1) integrate adaptation and mitigation strategies, 2) focus on the most vulnerable groups, 3) enhance the role of local knowledge in decision-making, 4) enhance community engagement, and 5) improve the quality and availability of data. The results of the interviews indicate that there is a need to 1) increase the focus on climate change in Mozambique, 2) enhance the capacity of actors to plan climate change interventions, 3) develop a climate change observatory, 4) adapt and adopt existing plans, and 5) increase the availability of finance for climate change interventions in Mozambique. The solutions proposed are multi-sectorial, and require both short-term and long-term strategies.

This thesis has several implications for practice and policy. It has implications for 1) researchers, 2) climate change practitioners, 3) climate change donors, 4) non-governmental organisations, 5) community-based organizations, 6) and the private sector. The thesis also has academic implications for 1) climate change intervention research and 2) systematic review methodology. The main contribution to knowledge is an understanding of the climate change intervention landscape in the Mozambique context.

The Eastern Cape province is the second-largest province in South Africa, and agriculture contributes 2.1% to its Gross Domestic Product (GDP) . Smallholder farmers contribute 49% of the total agricultural production in the province, and 96% of these farmers are subsistence farmers who practice multiple cropping . The Eastern Cape experiences droughts and floods every year, causing 95% crop yield and 100% livestock losses . This makes it difficult for the farmers to adopt new practices. This study was conducted in the Amathole district of the Eastern Cape, South Africa. The study site comprised of three sub-districts, namely, Ngqushwa, Great Kei and Buffalo City. The semi-structured questionnaire was based on the theoretical framework, which was adopted from the UTAINT model . The UTAINT model has got seven components, namely, 1) innovativeness, 2) adopter otherness, 3) access to information, 4) social network, and 5) time, 6) imitation and 7) facilitation. The model shows the inter-relationships between the components and their roles in the adoption process. The first component, innovativeness, is the outcome of the advantages of the innovation. The second component, adopter otherness, depends on the extent of the similarity or difference between the adopter and the innovator. The third component, access to information, is the availability and the level of knowledge about an innovation. Social network, the fourth component, is the communication structure among the farmers. Imitation, the sixth component, is the extent to which an individual learns from others and is imitative of others’ behaviour. The last component, facilitation, is the support that an individual receives from other farmers, and from other organisations. The framework is based on the principles of co-production of knowledge and builds on existing tools such as the Adaptation for Smallholder Agricultural Development (ASAD) framework, the Program for Accelerated Crop Improvement for African Agriculture (PACIA) and the System of Rice Intensification (SRI). The climate-smartness of 13 rice (Oryza spp.) and cowpea (Vigna unguiculata L. Walp.) interventions was assessed in site-specific field trials in Kenya, Nigeria, and Tanzania. The protocol consists of three interconnected stages: 1) planning and data collection, 2) data analysis and 3) knowledge co-production. During the planning stage, site-specific information such as climate data, agricultural practices, and crop characteristics are collected to determine the baseline climate-smartness of the interventions. During the data analysis stage, the climate-smartness of each intervention is scored by expert judges using a pre-validated 24-item questionnaire. Each item in the questionnaire is linked to one and sometimes two of the following climate-smart agriculture (CSA) principles: (i) increasing resilience to climate variability and extreme events, (ii) increasing productivity with limited use of natural resources, (iii) enhancing livelihoods, and (iv) mitigating greenhouse gas emissions, and the sub-principles contained therein. During the knowledge co-production stage, the results are discussed in a participatory process with the stakeholders to determine the potential of the interventions for enhancing CSA. The new protocol not only provides a quantitative assessment of the climate-smartness of the interventions but also facilitates a participatory process for planning and selecting the right combination of interventions for CSA. The protocol is thus ideally suited for the climate-smart planning and implementation of agricultural interventions in smallholder systems.

The CSA indicators are aligned with the Comprehensive Food Security and Vulnerability Analysis (CFSVA) framework and the Household Level Food Security Measurement Tool (HFI) used in the Ethiopia CSA and Nutrition project. The indices were normalized using z-scores to allow easy comparison of results across countries.

The concept is a broad one, but it has been embraced by the African Seed Access and Policy Innovation (ASAPI) project, which is working to develop policies and practical approaches to help smallholder farmers in Uganda and Ethiopia use climate-smart agricultural practices.

The project is a five-year partnership between the Earth Innovation Institute, the Alliance for a Green Revolution in Africa, the International Food Policy Research Institute, and the Technical Centre for Agricultural and Rural Cooperation. It is funded by the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation.

The term “climate smart” is a label applied to approaches to agriculture that not only help the people farming, but also mitigate climate change, and are sustainable.

These approaches can be as simple as encouraging farmers to plant trees around their farms, which can mean the difference between a good harvest and utter crop failure, or as complex as developing new varieties of crops that can survive a drought.

In developing these new approaches, researchers need access to certain seeds, which may already exist or ones that need to be developed.

This is where the ASAPI project comes in.

In Ethiopia, researchers are working to develop new crop varieties.

“We are identifying underexploited sources of heat and drought tolerance in both major food security crops in Ethiopia, such as maize and rice, and in lesser-known crops such as finger millet and sorghum,” said Elizabeth Mullinax, who is leading the variety development work in ASAPI.

In Uganda, the focus is on policies that support smallholder farmers.

“We are assessing policies that affect farmers’ ability to use climate-smart agriculture practices, and developing guidance to help policymakers better support farmers in adopting these practices,” said ASAPI policy specialist, Eric Mapondo.

The project also supports the capacity of the private seed sector to serve the needs of farmers.

“We are supporting the development of national seed strategies that ensure a continued supply of quality seed for farmers to adopt these new climate-smart agricultural practices,” said ASAPI’s private sector specialist, Dan Gies.

The authors also looked at the relationship between the interventions’ impact on individuals and the people they live with. They found that the people who benefited from the interventions also shared the benefits with others in their social networks.

For example, in one intervention in Uganda, a man received goats to help his family eat more meat. The man was then able to give some goats away to family and friends. A woman in Indonesia who received a chicken was able to give one away to a relative.

The authors note that this “spillover” effect is important for agencies setting policy and designing programs. If an intervention has a spillover effect, it can help people who aren’t directly targeted by the intervention. This can happen when people who benefit from an intervention share their good fortune with others in their community.

The authors also note that the opposite can happen. If people are only able to benefit from an intervention up to a certain point, an increase in their benefit might actually cause them to share less with others. For example, if a cash transfer program allows a person to lift themselves and their family out of poverty, the program has benefited them greatly. But if they then experience a second increase in income, that additional income might make them feel less dependent on the people in their social network. This could cause them to share less with the people they live with.

The authors note that it’s important for agencies to design programs that promote “spillover” effects and avoid situations where people might become less likely to share with others.

First Online:

Cite this article as:

Botha, W., 2019, ‘Pathogens of Vertebrate Animals as Invasive Species: Insights from South Africa’, Suid-Afrikaanse Tydskrif vir Natuurwetenskap en Tegnologie 38(1), a1539. https://doi.org/10.4102/satnt.v38i1.1539

Pathogens of Vertebrate Animals as Invasive Species: Insights from South Africa

Received: 31 July 2018; Accepted: 19 Feb. 2019; Published: 28 Aug. 2019

The pathogens of vertebrate animals are increasingly being recognised as invasive species. The definition of an invasive species is not entirely straightforward, but generally an invasive species is an introduced species that has a negative impact on an ecosystem. This article discusses the degree to which pathogens of vertebrate animals can be regarded as invasive species, using South Africa as a case in point. The article concludes that pathogens can be regarded as invasive species if the following criteria are met: the pathogen must be introduced to a new environment, must be able to reproduce and survive in the new environment, must be able to find and infect a host and must have a negative impact on the new environment. The article further concludes that the introduction of a pathogen into a new environment can be either natural or anthropogenic. The anthropogenic introduction of pathogens can be done intentionally or unintentionally. The introduction of pathogens can also be the result of anthropogenic climate change. The geographic range of pathogens can be expanded by the anthropogenic movement of vertebrate animals. The pathogens of vertebrate animals can be regarded as invasive species in at least two ways: directly, when the pathogen is introduced into a new environment; and indirectly, when the pathogen is introduced into a new environment due to a change in the geographic range of the host animal. The geographic range of the host animal can change due to anthropogenic climate change, overexploitation of the host population by humans or the intentional or unintentional introduction of the host animal into a new environment. The article ends by highlighting some of the problems associated with the recognition of pathogens as invasive species and by indicating some of the potential management strategies to deal with invasive pathogens.

Keywords: Invasive species; pathogens; vertebrate animals; South Africa.

This is surprising given that the impact and spread of alien species is in many ways similar to that of infectious diseases. Here, we examine the history, present status and future directions of this research topic, highlighting its importance and suggesting avenues for further research. The study of alien species as diseases has a long history, but this was not considered in invasion science until quite recently. A small but growing body of literature now exists, which demonstrates that infectious disease concepts can be applied to the study of alien species, and vice versa, and that this combined approach has the potential to increase our understanding of both biological invasions and infectious disease dynamics. We propose that a key difference between alien species and many infectious diseases is the extent of dispersal that is required for invasion or disease emergence. In addition, we suggest that the threat of alien species to native biodiversity is potentially greater than that of infectious diseases to humans, and highlight the need and opportunities for more research that compares these two areas of biology.

The last case of rinderpest in Kenya was recorded in 2001, and the disease has been officially declared eradicated from Africa in 2010. The virus that causes rinderpest is genetically very similar to that which causes cattle fever, a disease that still affects cattle worldwide and represents a serious threat to the health of domesticated cattle. The eradication of rinderpest from Africa has therefore provided an excellent opportunity to test strategies aimed at preventing the spread of cattle fever to the continent. In particular, it offers an opportunity to assess the likelihood that cattle fever may be eradicated from Africa in a similar time frame. Our results suggest that the eradication of cattle fever is a realistic goal, provided that appropriate attention is given to the control of the disease in key endemic countries and to the need to maintain a high level of vigilance in those countries where the disease has already been eradicated. If the global eradication of cattle fever is achieved, it will represent a significant public health accomplishment, and a service to both wildlife and domesticated cattle.

Source: https://www.news.utoronto.ca

News Release

What scientists know about microscopic invaders that cause disease in South Africa

April 21, 2022

New research provides a comprehensive overview of the pathogens causing disease in the country

A new U of T Mississauga-led review provides a comprehensive overview of the pathogens causing disease in South Africa, and highlights the urgent need for continued research to better understand the impact of these microscopic invaders.

The review, published today in the journal Pathogens, was led by University of Toronto Mississauga Professor Sherrill Evans and University of KwaZulu-Natal Professor Thirumala Govender. It provides a comprehensive overview of the pathogens causing disease in the country, with a focus on those that are drug-resistant and those that could be spread by ticks.

“South Africa is considered a hot spot for emerging and re-emerging pathogens, which are responsible for a wide range of diseases in humans, from malaria and HIV/AIDS to rabies and tick-borne relapsing fever,” said Evans, a professor in the Department of Chemistry & Chemical Biology and the Department of Physics & Astronomy.

Evans and Govender are both members of the Global Health Institute at U of T Mississauga.

The review highlights the urgent need for continued research to better understand the impact of these microscopic invaders.

“Understanding the diversity of the pathogens causing disease in South Africa is essential for the implementation of public health policies and disease surveillance programs,” said Govender, a professor in the School of Laboratory Medicine & Medical Sciences at the University of KwaZulu-Natal.

The review also emphasizes the importance of tick-borne pathogens, which have received relatively little attention in South Africa. Ticks are known to transmit a variety of pathogens in South Africa, including bacteria that cause relapsing fever and Lyme disease, and a virus that causes Powassan fever.

“While there has been a lot of research on tick-borne pathogens in North America and Europe, there is still a lot we don’t know about tick-borne pathogens in South Africa,” said Evans. “This is particularly concerning because the tick that transmits the Lyme disease bacterium in North America and Europe – Ixodes scapularis – is very similar to the tick that transmits the relapsing fever bacterium in South Africa – Ixodes ricinus. If these ticks come into contact with the Lyme disease bacterium, it could have serious health consequences for people in South Africa.”

The researchers wanted to know how the animals and people in the area were exposed to the viruses. They tested blood and tissue samples from 243 people living in the area, and from 464 cattle. The work appeared in mBio, an open-access journal from ASM.

The researchers found that the people had antibodies to all three viruses, indicating past infections. Antibodies are proteins that the immune system produces, to help fight off future infections with the same virus. The cattle also had antibodies to all three viruses, and in addition, in some cases, to viruses not yet found in the area. The researchers also found RNA from all three viruses in the blood of some people. This result indicates that the people may have been recently infected, or that they were recently vaccinated against the viruses.

“Having all three viruses in the same location is really unusual and probably the cause of multiple infections in people and animals,” says Maria J. de Vries, a virologist at the University of Pretoria in South Africa, who was not involved in the work. “This is the first study that gives molecular evidence of all three viruses in people and animals living in the same area. It confirms that the high exposure of the population to these viruses is not limited to one specific animal species.” de Vries says that the work shows that the viruses are being transmitted between different animal species, which could be a sign of virus adaptation to the environment.

The work also shows that the viruses are not being transmitted at a high rate. For example, the researchers calculated that people were 12.5 times more likely to be infected with RVF than with Nipah, and that cattle were 25 times more likely to be infected with Nipah than with Hendra. “This suggests that for now, these viruses don’t transmit easily from animals to people or from one animal species to another,” says Ronald F. Ross Jr., a virologist at the University of Texas Medical Branch in Galveston, who was not involved in the work.

The researchers note that the work does not indicate who or what is infecting the other. “Our data cannot be used to determine the route of virus exposure, whether from animals to people or from people to animals, or from which specific animal species the infection was acquired,” they write. Further studies could reveal how these viruses are spreading in the area, which could help prevent future infections.

Invasive species are often used as biological control agents against invasive plants, but they can also cause harm to native species and the environment. In a recent study, researchers from Chalmers University of Technology, Sweden, have investigated how invasive species can be used in a responsible way. Their conclusion is that we need to know more about the species before we use them, and that we need to monitor the effects when they are used. The researchers have presented their findings in the journal BioMed Central’s journal, BMC Biology.

Invasive species have been used as biological control agents (BCAs) to control invasive plants, because they are host specific and will not cause harm to the environment. However, there is a lack of knowledge about how to use them in a responsible way. Therefore, Anna Lönnstedt, Biologist at the Department of Biology and Natural Environment at Chalmers University of Technology, Sweden, together with her colleagues, has conducted a study to try to find out how to increase the likelihood that using invasive species as BCAs will have a positive outcome.

The researchers have investigated three aspects that they think are important when considering whether or not to use invasive species as BCAs: 1) the probability of success, 2) the risk for negative impacts on native species and the environment, and 3) the responsibility of the scientist. One of the most important findings is that more information is needed before invasive species are used as BCAs. The researchers suggest that the species should be used only when there is a high probability of success. However, there are many factors that affect the probability of success, and more information is needed to determine these factors. Therefore, the scientists should monitor the effects when the species are used. This is the first step towards “responsible invasion science”.

Anna Lönnstedt says: “Our conclusion is that we do not know enough about the species before we use them, and therefore we need to monitor the effects when they are used as biological control agents against invasive plants. samples.hyp:
in pediatric age group: A modified protocol

Background: Odontogenic Keratocyst (OK) is a relatively rare disorder with cystic appearance having high recurrence rate. Multimodal approach and modal treatment approach are two treatment modalities used commonly in management of OK. Multimodal approach includes enucleation, cryosurgery, curettage and electrosurgery. Modal treatment approach includes enucleation with/without cryosurgery, curettage with/without electrosurgery and cryosurgery with/without electrosurgery. There is no well defined treatment protocol for OK in pediatric age group. The aim of this study was to evaluate the efficacy of a modified protocol for management of OK in pediatric age group.
Methods: A prospective cohort study was conducted on 60 patients of age group 8-16 years with a mean age of 11.2 years. Patients with a clinical and radiographic evidence of OK were included in the study. Patients were followed up after surgery for 24 months. OK was managed according to a modified protocol. The modified protocol included enucleation with/without cryosurgery, curettage with/without electrosurgery and cryosurgery with/without electrosurgery. Data was collected and analyzed by SPSS version 20.
Results: Out of 60 patients, 43 (71.66%) were male and 17 (28.33%) were female with a male to female ratio of 2.5:1. Out of 60 OKs managed, 23 (38.33%) were managed by enucleation alone, 19 (31.66%) by enucleation with cryosurgery, 16 (26.66%) by curettage with electrosurgery and 2 (3.33%) by cryosurgery with electrosurgery. Recurrence was observed in 8 (13.33%) patients during 24 months of follow up.
Conclusion: A modified protocol of multimodal approach had high success rate and was well tolerated in management of OK in pediatric age group.

English:
English: Background: Odontogenic keratocyst (OK) is a relatively rare, non-neoplastic, cystic lesion that can recur after complete clinical and radiographic healing.
English: Objective: The purpose of this systematic review is to synthesize the current evidence and provide recommendations for the management of odontogenic keratocyst.
English: Material and Methods: A systematic search of the electronic databases PubMed, Medline, EMBASE, Scopus, and Web of Science for articles published to date was conducted. The search was performed by one reviewer and independently verified by another. Disagreements were resolved by discussion. The methodological quality of the studies was evaluated using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS) for cohort studies and the Risk of Bias Assessment Tool (ROB 2.0) for randomized controlled trials (RCTs). Based on the evidence generated from the included studies, management options were discussed and recommendations made.
English: Results: Twenty-one studies were included in this review, which assessed the efficacy of different treatment modalities, including surgery alone, surgery with adjuvant therapy, and observation alone. According to the NOS, six studies were rated as high quality and nine as moderate. According to the ROB 2.0, three RCTs were rated as high risk of bias. Complete clinical and radiographic healing was reported after surgical treatment alone in 53.6% of cases and was not associated with any specific surgical technique. The use of adjuvant therapy resulted in healing rates of 71.4%–100% and was significantly associated with a lower recurrence rate compared with surgery alone.

samples.ref: Maganin Sars-CoV-2 (2019-nCoV), MERS-CoV da kuma rigakafin SARSr-CoV: Nazarin ƙididdiga na kwatanci don bayar da shawarar masu motsa amsawar garkuwar jiki jiki da suka dace
samples.hyp:
for vaccine design

The ongoing COVID-19 pandemic caused by the novel coronavirus SARS-CoV-2 has affected the entire world and resulted in a severe public health crisis. The development of effective vaccines is one of the most urgent tasks of the scientific community at the moment. However, the design of a vaccine is challenging due to the length of the epitopes, high conservation level of the spike protein, and its possible immunogenicity. Therefore, there is an urgent need to develop computational methods that can predict immunogenic epitopes for the design of a synthetic peptide vaccine. In this study, we performed a comparative analysis of SARS-CoV-2 with SARS-CoV and MERS-CoV and identified 6 epitopes of 15-mers length that were epitopes common to all three viruses. In addition, 43 epitopes specific to SARS-CoV-2 and 12 epitopes specific to MERS-CoV were identified. We were able to propose candidate epitopes for vaccine design against all three viruses. The selection of the most suitable epitopes for the design of a peptide vaccine against SARS-CoV-2 and the improvement of the methods for the prediction of immunogenicity will be the next important steps in the design of a synthetic peptide vaccine against SARS-CoV-2.

Keywords: Computational biology; Peptide vaccine; S protein; epitope prediction; SARS-CoV- 2; MERS-CoV; protein structure prediction.

A new study is the first to analyze SARS-CoV-2 genomes from the first few months of the pandemic in relation to five related viruses.

This research could help scientists develop better treatments and vaccines for Covid-19.

The virus that causes Covid-19 is a coronavirus. Scientists have now compared the SARS-CoV-2 virus to five similar viruses to see if it has any features in common with them.

The viruses were compared at the genetic level.

- SARS-CoV

- SARS-CoV-1

- OC43

- NL63

- 229E

The study found that SARS-CoV-2 is most closely related to NL63.

samples.hyp:
The study aimed to systematically review and meta-analysis of the available evidence on the prevalence of cardiac arrhythmias in patients with COVID-19 to better understand the incidence of cardiac arrhythmias in patients with COVID-19 infection and to highlight the publication bias in this regard.

The search was performed in the PubMed, EMBASE, and SCOPUS databases until March 2021. The prevalence of cardiac arrhythmias in patients with COVID-19 was summarized, and publication bias was assessed by funnel plot and Egger’s regression model.

The incidence of cardiac arrhythmias was reported in 44 out of 2240 studies. The prevalence of cardiac arrhythmias in patients with COVID-19 was 19% [very low quality evidence, I2 = 87.76%, 95% confidence interval (CI): 14%-26%]. The funnel plot showed no evidence of publication bias (Egger’s regression intercept = -1.90, 95% CI: -5.63 to 1.83, p = 0.34). This study revealed that patients with COVID-19 had a high incidence of cardiac arrhythmias, and the incidence of bradycardia and atrial fibrillation was 10% and 3%, respectively.

Arrhythmias are a known complication of COVID-19. Patients with reduced left ventricular ejection fraction and abnormal renal and liver function are more likely to develop arrhythmias. If these patients receive SARS-CoV-2 vaccination, antiarrhythmic drugs should be given with caution because of the increased risk of drug-induced arrhythmias.

This study aimed to summarize the current understanding of the arrhythmogenic potential of SARS-CoV-2 and to provide an overview of the reported incidence of arrhythmias in COVID-19 patients. A comprehensive search was performed in PubMed, EMBASE, and Web of Science for articles reporting the incidence of arrhythmias in COVID-19 patients. The search strategy was updated on the 11th of October 2020 and limited to articles published in English. The title and abstract of all retrieved articles were screened; duplicates and irrelevant articles were removed. The full-text of the remaining articles was examined. Discrepancies between reviewers were resolved through discussion. A total of 7605 articles were identified, of which 93 articles were included in the final synthesis. The incidence of arrhythmias was reported in 19.2% (95% CI 16.8-21.6%) of COVID-19 patients. In hospitalized patients, arrhythmias were observed in 20.4% (95% CI 18.6-22.2%) and 16.7% (95% CI 15.3-18.1%) in non-hospitalized patients. Supraventricular tachyarrhythmias were the most prevalent arrhythmias in COVID-19 patients. The overall mortality rate was 16.1% (95% CI 13.8-18.6%) in patients with arrhythmias and 2.7% (95% CI 2.4-3.2%) in patients without arrhythmias. Patients with atrial fibrillation or flutter had a higher mortality rate of 33.4% (95% CI 25.1-42.9%) than patients with normal sinus rhythm (2.2% (95% CI 1.5-3.1%)). This summary of the current evidence suggests that arrhythmias, especially atrial fibrillation or flutter, are not rare in patients with COVID-19, especially in hospitalized patients, and are associated with a higher risk of mortality.

This study is a single-center retrospective cohort study, conducted in a tertiary care facility in the north of Italy between March and May 2020. We included all consecutive patients aged ≥18 years admitted to the cardiology department with a diagnosis of SARS-CoV-2 infection confirmed by polymerase chain reaction. The main outcome measure was the incidence of arrhythmias, and arrhythmic emergencies. The secondary outcome measure was the length of hospital and ICU stay. 121 patients were included, 83 (68.7%) were male, the median age was 57 (IQR 40-68), 111 (91.8%) had at least one pre-existing comorbidity, and 95 (78.5%) had been previously hospitalized. The median time between the onset of symptoms and the patient’s admission to our hospital was 9 days (IQR 6-13). 50 (41.3%) patients had no cardiovascular history. 29 (24%) patients developed any type of arrhythmia, 16 (13.2%) had atrial fibrillation, 13 (10.8%) developed new onset heart failure, and 5 (4.1%) died. 6 (5.5%) patients developed new-onset ventricular arrhythmias (5 monomorphic ventricular tachycardia and 1 polymorphic ventricular tachycardia), and 4 (3.3%) had a ventricular arrhythmic emergency (3 hemodynamically stable monomorphic ventricular tachycardia and 1 polymorphic ventricular fibrillation). The patients with arrhythmic emergencies were significantly more likely to be in shock (p = 0.002) and require mechanical ventilation (p < 0.001). The median length of hospital and ICU stay was 9 days (IQR 7-13) and 11 days (IQR 7-15), respectively. In this cohort of patients with COVID-19 admitted to a tertiary referral center, arrhythmias, in particular ventricular arrhythmias, occurred in a relevant proportion of patients.

The most common arrhythmia is atrial fibrillation (AF), a quivering or rapid and irregular heartbeat that can lead to blood clots, stroke, and heart failure. 

AF affects about 33 million people worldwide, and that number is expected to rise to 56 million by 2030. 

It is often asymptomatic, so early detection is difficult. 

A new study published in the Journal of the American Heart Association looked at whether an AI-powered ECG could detect AF more effectively than traditional ECGs.

Researchers in China analyzed data from 9,601 patients who were referred for ECGs to rule out cardiovascular diseases. 

Of these, 1,006 had AF. 

The AI algorithm was able to identify AF in ECGs with a sensitivity of 95.8% and specificity of 99.3%, which is much higher than the 70% and 90% rates achieved by human ECG readers.

The study shows that AI can be a valuable tool for AF detection, but it comes with some caveats. 

First, although the AI algorithm was highly accurate, it still missed some cases of AF, so it is not yet ready to replace human ECG readers. 

Second, the AI algorithm was only as good as the data it was trained on, so it is important to ensure that the dataset is representative of the population it will be used on. 

Finally, while AI can assist with AF detection, it should not be used as a replacement for regular medical check-ups. 

AF is a serious condition that can lead to other health problems, so it is important to catch it early with a traditional ECG. 

In the future, AI-powered ECGs could be a valuable addition to traditional ECGs, but for now, it is important to strike a balance and use both for optimal results.

However, a few studies have suggested that post-migration stressors have a stronger effect on the mental health of migrants and refugees. The current study aimed to investigate the relative effect of pre- and post-migration stressors on the mental health of a sample of Arab refugees who were hosted in the Palestinian society, and to examine the moderating effect of post-migration stressors on the association between pre-migration stressors and mental health. This study was conducted using the cross-sectional design with the sample of 1006 Arab refugees hosted in the Palestinian refugee camps in the Gaza Strip. The participants were administered a set of self-report questionnaires, which included the Pre-Migration Stress Scale (PMSS), the Post-Migration Stress Scale (PMS), and the Symptom Checklist -90-Revised (SCL-90-R). The results of multiple regression analysis indicated that post-migration stressors explained a greater variance in mental health than pre-migration stressors. Moreover, post-migration stressors were found to strengthen the association between pre-migration stressors and mental health. The findings of this study provide important evidence on the impact of stressors on the mental health of refugees. The findings suggest that the mental health interventions for refugees should focus on reducing the stressors and on developing the refugee's ability to cope with the stressors.

The mental health of newly arrived refugees is affected by the situation they left behind and by the challenges of settling in a new place, according to a study carried out at Umeå University in Sweden.

The study shows that it is not only the refugees’ own experiences during flight and the conditions in the country of asylum that affect their mental health, but also the circumstances in the region from which they came and the cultural differences between the refugees’ country of origin and their new host country.

This is due to the traumatic events they experience in their home country, during flight, and upon arrival at their destination. Many seek help from psychotherapy, and medication. However, access to health services is not always available. This is especially true for refugees and migrants who are living in developing countries. In a recent study, researchers examined whether virtual reality (VR) exposure therapy could be a viable option to enhance mental health treatment for refugees and migrants. The study was conducted in cooperation with the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) and was conducted in cooperation with the UNHCR and the World Health Organization (WHO).

VR exposure therapy

In VR exposure therapy, patients visit traumatic events in a safe virtual environment, which can be adjusted to match the patient’s specific needs and fears. This form of therapy has already shown promise in treating post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and other anxiety-related conditions. However, it has not yet been studied in refugee populations. In the recent study, researchers wanted to investigate whether VR exposure therapy could be an effective addition to mental health treatment for refugees and migrants.

The researchers recruited 75 refugees, who lived in a rural area of Uganda and had experienced trauma. The refugees were randomly assigned to one of three groups. Two of the groups received eight sessions of mental health treatment. The first group received treatment as usual, which consisted of mental health group sessions led by trained counselors. The second group received treatment as usual plus four sessions of VR exposure therapy. The third group did not receive any VR treatment. All of the VR exposure therapy sessions were conducted by trained counselors using the HTC Vive virtual reality system, which is a headset that projects the VR images into the real world. The VR exposure therapy was designed to address specific fears that refugees often experience, such as fear of specific animals, personal safety, and social situations. The researchers then measured changes in the participants’ mental health symptoms, such as fear, distress, and PTSD symptoms, before and after treatment.

The results of the study showed that, compared to the control group, both groups that received treatment as usual plus VR exposure therapy had significant reductions in symptoms. This suggests that VR exposure therapy may be a promising new tool for improving mental health treatment for refugees and migrants. However, the researchers note that more research is needed to confirm these findings and to determine the long-term effects of VR exposure therapy. They also plan to conduct further research to improve the VR exposure therapy protocol and to test its effectiveness in other refugee populations.

The following are some of the most common symptoms of PTSD. Not everyone with PTSD will have all of these symptoms, and some people may have very different symptoms. Symptoms may also come and go over time.

1. Reliving the event (also called re-experiencing symptoms). This is one of the most common types of symptoms. Reliving symptoms may include:
  • Bad dreams or flashbacks about the event
  •Reliving parts of the event, like hearing or seeing things that happened
  •Disturbing thoughts about the event

2. Avoiding situations that remind you of the event. This type of symptom can cause people to avoid places, events, or objects that remind them of the traumatic event. This can include anything from driving past the place where the event happened to seeing something on TV that is a reminder of the event. Avoiding situations is a common way to cope, but it only makes the problem worse in the long run by keeping a person from getting help and preventing them from learning to think about the event in a healthy way.

3. Being very sensitive to certain senses. For example, if you were in a car accident, the smell of gasoline or the sound of a siren can bring back bad memories of the accident. This is called having a sensory trigger. Some people may also be very sensitive to certain tastes, textures, or smells.

The researchers noted that the results highlight the need for a more holistic approach to supporting migrants, and that migrants themselves should be involved in the design and implementation of such approaches.

The researchers explained that this is the first time that such a comprehensive study has been carried out of the mental health of young migrants in the UK, and it will help inform the development of future mental health services for this group. They added that it is also the first time that the study has been carried out in such close collaboration with local authorities, who collected the data for the study, and say that this partnership approach is crucial for the success of future studies like this. Professor Tanya Byron, who chairs the Department of Health’s Chief Medical Officer’s Expert Group on the Mental Health and Wellbeing of Children and Young People, commented “This research provides a snapshot of the mental health of young migrants in the UK and highlights the fact that many experience mental health difficulties. The research also shows that the longer young migrants spend in the UK, the better their mental health. This is an important finding as it shows that time does help. However, it is important that we learn more about what it is about the longer time spent in the UK that is beneficial to their mental health. In addition, we need to ensure that the services that are available for young migrants are as comprehensive as they are effective.”

Dr. Thomas Protheroe, Birkbeck’s Head of Psychology, added “Mental health is everyone’s business, and it is vital that those who are responsible for the care and well-being of migrants, from social workers to doctors and nurses, as well as young migrants themselves, understand the mental health difficulties that migrants experience. This research helps to identify the factors which contribute to mental health problems in young migrants, and will help the development of interventions which are targeted at addressing these problems.”

Dr. Vostanek is now working with Dr. Protheroe and a number of colleagues at Birkbeck and other institutions on a number of follow-up projects that will address some of the issues highlighted by this research. These include a large scale study to examine the mental health of young male migrants (ages 16-24), and a study that will examine the mental health of unaccompanied migrant children who were separated from their parents.

The paper, “Mental health and wellbeing of adolescent migrants in the UK: A comparative study of young people with and without refugee experience”, is published in the journal Children and Youth Services Review.

The book chapter on which this article is based was written by Dr James Gibbs, a former visiting fellow at the IES and current lecturer at the University of Cape Town, and Dr Thomas Luedl, a former visiting fellow at the IES and current senior lecturer at the University of Wits. The ethnographic study on which the chapter is based was conducted by Gibbs while at the IES. The ethnographic study included participant observation of a local Ghanaian social club in Germany, as well as semi-structured interviews with a sample of Ghanaians living in Germany. The chapter focuses on the strategies that Ghanaian migrants use to remain in contact with relatives back home. It argues that migrants’ reliance on social networks of family and friends, as well as new media communication technologies, challenges the notion that migrants are becoming increasingly ‘deterritorialized’ and ‘deracinated’.

The primary objective of this study was to determine the prevalence of HW in asymptomatic cattle in Botswana. A total of 563 cattle from 12 farms in three districts of Botswana were sampled during the winter season of 2018. The three districts are: Ngami in the North-Western part of the country, Bobonong in the Southern part and Mahalapye in the Central District. About 5 ml of blood was collected from the jugular vein and used to extract DNA using the TIAGEN Blood/Body Fluid DNA Kit. The presence of HW was detected using the real-time polymerase chain reaction (PCR). Of the 563 cattle, 65 (11.53%) were positive for HW. Of the 35 farms, 20 (57.14%) were positive for HW. The HW infection was significantly associated with age (P<0.0001) with 41 (18.64%) out of 220 adult cattle being positive for HW compared to 24 (9.38%) out of 257 young cattle. There was no significant association between the prevalence of HW and farm size (P = 0.6349), season (P = 0.3736) and tsetse fly challenge (P = 0.60). This study is the first to report on the prevalence of HW in cattle in Botswana. The overall prevalence of 11.53% suggests that HW is endemic in the country and poses a potential threat to the cattle industry. These results suggest that preventive measures need to be taken to protect the cattle industry from the adverse effects of HW.

samples.src: This study gives a view of the epidemiological burden of heartwater in Botswana.
samples.ref: Wannan binciken yana ba da ra'ayi game da nauyin cutar kumburin zuciya a cikin ƙasar Botswana.
samples.hyp:
Heartwater is caused by the protozoan parasite Cardia olstoni, transmitted by the brown ear tick, Amblyomma variegatum. The study was a retrospective study from 2007 to 2016. A cross-sectional study was conducted in 2016. A total of 4290 ticks were collected from 179 cattle. The ticks were identified to the species level, screened for the presence of heartwater antigen, and serologically tested for the presence of heartwater antibody. The prevalence of the parasite was estimated in the ticks and cattle. The risk factors for the parasite in cattle were determined using univariable and multivariable logistic regression. A total of 4290 Amblyomma variegatum were collected from 179 cattle. Of the 4290 ticks, 63 (1.47%) were positive for heartwater antigen. Of the 63 positive ticks, 34 (53.8%) were female and 29 (46.2%) were male. Of the 179 cattle, 10 (5.6%) were positive for heartwater antibody. The overall prevalence of heartwater in ticks and cattle was 1.47% and 5.6%, respectively. The prevalence of the parasite was estimated to be 1.74% in ticks and 6.1% in cattle. Being >2 years of age was the only risk factor for heartwater in the univariable model, while being >2 years of age [odds ratio (OR) 3.9; 95% confidence interval (CI) 1.4–10.7], tick attachment >30 days [OR 6.2; 95% CI 2.7–14.0], and tick mass >0.1 g [OR 3.6; 95% CI 1.5–8.6] were found to be significant risk factors in the multivariable model. This study showed a low prevalence of heartwater in Botswana. The low prevalence can be attributed to the implementation of a tick-borne disease management program in the country. However, there was a low power of the study to detect the true prevalence of the parasite in cattle due to the small sample size. Further studies with a larger sample size are required to understand the epidemiology of the disease in the country.

The sub-districts were selected based on their ecological and climatic conditions. The collected ticks were identified to the lowest possible taxonomic level and fed on sheep for 24 hours. DNA was extracted from the engorged females and the cytochrome oxidase subunit 1 (COI) gene was amplified, sequenced and compared with sequences available in GenBank. A total of 94 ticks were collected. The genus Amblyomma was identified in all four sub-districts, while the genera Rhipicephalus and Hyalomma were only identified in two of the four sub-districts. Phylogenetic analysis of the COI gene sequences revealed that ticks from the four sub-districts belong to a group of previously described Rhipicephalus microplus from Zimbabwe and Botswana. The study showed that the feeding behaviour of the collected ticks was influenced by the environmental conditions of the sub-districts. The results of this study contribute to the knowledge of the tick fauna of Southern Botswana and will help to design control strategies for tick-borne diseases in livestock.

Heartwater is caused by the protozoan parasite, Cardiaboldes elomys, which is transmitted by the brown ear-tick, Rhipicephalus appendiculatus. The disease is characterized by anemia, congested liver, edema, and a sero-salivary response. In this study, we screened 1,860 cattle for Cardiaboldes elomys infection using the indirect fluorescent antibody test. Ticks were collected from cattle and counted. Heartwater was confirmed in 11 of the 48 villages surveyed in southern Botswana. The prevalence of infection in cattle was 6.7% (12/180) in Ngwaketse, 2.3% (4/180) in Takatokwane, 5.6% (10/180) in Mmathethe, 1.1% (2/180) in Moshupa, 17.5% (28/160) in Mabutsane, and 9.1% (16/180) in Mahalapye. The overall prevalence of infection was 8.2%. The brown ear-tick, Rhipicephalus appendiculatus, was the most abundant tick on cattle and was found in all study sites at prevalences ranging from 71.4% to 100%. Our findings highlight the widespread nature of ticks and heartwater in Botswana, which poses a threat to the country’s cattle industry.

samples.hyp:
The disease is spread when an infected tick bites and sucks blood from an animal. Heartwater is one of the most important diseases of livestock in sub-Saharan Africa, where it causes major economic losses due to abortion and death of pregnant animals, and reduced weight gain in young animals. There are no effective vaccines against the disease. The best way to prevent heartwater is to treat animals with acaricides, which kill ticks, and to test for the presence of the bacteria in blood. However, acaricides are relatively expensive, and are not always available in remote areas. Also, acaricides kill only the ticks on the treated animal, and do not control ticks in the environment, meaning that ticks from other animals can still transmit the disease. In this study, we want to examine whether cattle can be protected against heartwater infection if they are fed a diet containing heat-killed E. ruminantium bacteria, or a control diet. We will test the efficacy of the diets at different time points after tick bite exposure. We will also examine how the diet affects the immune response of the animal to the infection. The results from this study will provide us with information on whether feeding heat-killed E. ruminantium bacteria has the potential to protect against heartwater infection in cattle, which would be an inexpensive and novel strategy for heartwater control.

The disease is caused by a parasite that is transmitted by ticks. The parasite is present in the blood of infected animals and is transmitted to uninfected animals when ticks feed on the animal’s blood. The disease is known as “heartwater” because the parasite damages the lining of small blood vessels in the heart, causing the heart to expand and press on other organs, from which the animal may die. The disease is found in West Africa, from Senegal eastward to Sudan, and southward to Ivory Coast and Ethiopia. It is not found in North Africa or the Near East. The disease does not occur in South America, although both the parasite and the tick that transmits the parasite are found in Central and South America. The disease is a major constraint to livestock production in West Africa, and has the potential to cause severe economic losses in new areas where it is currently not found. The disease can also infect humans, causing a relapsing fever. The main sign of human heartwater is fatigue. The disease is treatable with antibiotics. Several vaccines for use in livestock have been developed, but none are currently being used in the United States. The disease is not transmitted from livestock to humans or from livestock to poultry.

“We found that the number of infective ticks that feed on an animal is critical to the likelihood of an animal getting heartwater,” says Dr. Collins Oduor, a postdoctoral researcher at ILRI affiliated with the University of Nairobi. “We also found that the probability of an animal getting infected increases with the number of infective ticks in a herd and the distance that ticks can disperse from the herd,” he adds.

These findings suggest that the risk of heartwater in an area depends on the number of infected ticks, the distance they can travel, and how many ticks feed on an animal.

“Understanding how the parasite is transmitted is key to being able to control the disease,” says Dr. Ann Mwangangi, a postdoctoral researcher at KLRI affiliated with the Kenya Ministry of Health. “This knowledge could help inform policies to manage and control heartwater,” she adds.

The researchers found that the risk of an animal getting heartwater is low where fewer than 100 infective ticks carrying the parasite are present and ticks travel less than 500 meters from the host.

However, where there are more than 100 infective ticks in a 10-square-kilometer area, or where ticks can travel more than 500 meters from the host, the risk of an animal getting heartwater increases significantly. In such areas, at least 50 percent of the ticks would need to be treated to reduce the risk of disease to that of areas with lower tick numbers and shorter tick dispersal.

It is characterised by fever, loss of appetite, depression, and oedema.

The disease is currently a major constraint to livestock production and trade in southern Africa. It is endemic in several countries in west and central Africa, and has been reported from Nigeria to Sudan and Kenya to Mozambique.

It was first discovered in Zimbabwe in 1900, and in Botswana at the end of the 19th century.

The researchers said the disease has been reported in Botswana, but has not been studied in depth. 

“We found that the prevalence of heartwater in the study area was high,” they wrote. 

They attributed the re-emergence of the disease to the introduction of ticks that act as vectors for the disease. 

“[This was] due to the increase in ticks, most probably as a result of the favourable climatic conditions, which have led to a significant increase in the tick vector, Amblyomma variegatum,” they wrote. 

They recommended increased surveillance for the disease, and early reporting of cases to prevent the further spread of the disease. 

They also recommended the implementation of a national tick-borne disease surveillance network to enable early detection of emerging tick-borne diseases in Botswana.

The study has been published in the “Tropical Animal Health and Production” journal.

The team of researchers included Botswana-based academics from the University of Botswana and the Botswana University of Agriculture and Natural Resources.

Others were based in Israel and South Africa.

"This is the first time we have looked at the spatial distribution of ticks and the relationship between tick distribution and heartwater cases in Botswana," said Dr. Alfredo Aguilar-Souza, an assistant professor and epidemiologist at the University of Botswana's School of Public Health and a study co-author. "We found there is a positive correlation between the density of ticks and the prevalence of heartwater."

Heartwater is transmitted by ticks and can cause fatal disease in livestock, which can lead to food insecurity and loss of livelihood for farmers. The disease can be transmitted to humans, causing symptoms such as fever, headache, general malaise and arthralgia. The study found that 13.24 percent of ticks were infected with the heartwater pathogen.

"Understanding the geographical distribution of ticks and the relationship between tick density and the prevalence of heartwater will help authorities plan surveillance activities and implement control measures," said Dr. Samuel Vruthan, research coordinator for the University of Pretoria's Department of Parasitology and director of the Tick-Borne Pathogens Research Unit at the University of Pretoria's Faculty of Veterinary Science.

The study was published recently in the African Journal of Biomedical Research.

However, the implementation of POC tests in sub-Saharan Africa has been slow. Here, we describe the development of a portable, low-cost, rapid (15 minutes), lateral flow, point-of-care test (POCT) for the qualitative detection of antibodies to HIV-1 and HIV-2 in human serum, plasma, and whole blood. The test is based on the principle of double antigen sandwich followed by visual detection of colored particles. The sensitivity and specificity of the test were 98.76% and 99.77%, respectively. The results of this study suggest that the test can be used for screening and confirmatory testing of HIV-1 and HIV-2. The test could be an effective tool for use by non-trainable individuals in remote areas and resource limited settings including the home. Therefore, the test could play a key role in the elimination of transmission of mother to child and from person to person. The test could also be used for patient self-testing. The test is quick, and provides results within 15 minutes, which is adequate for both the patient and the healthcare provider. In addition, the test is simple to operate and does not require expensive equipment, making it a cost-effective tool for healthcare providers in resource-limited settings. The test is storage stable for 24 months at room temperature and requires only minimal training to operate. The test is suitable for both mobile and fixed healthcare settings and can potentially contribute to the achievement of universal HIV testing in sub-Saharan Africa.

MedWire (London, UK): A point-of-care test for SARS-CoV-2 may allow clinicians to quickly diagnose patients and initiate treatment, according to news reported online in The Lancet.

The test, developed by Cepheid, is a real-time polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) test that uses nasal swabs. It has 100% sensitivity and 100% specificity for the detection of SARS-CoV-2, the virus that causes COVID-19, and takes approximately 45 minutes to generate a result.

‘The performance of this test in a real-world setting, at the point of care, is highly desirable to rapidly and accurately support clinical management decisions,’ comment Michael Osterholm (University of Minnesota, USA) and colleagues in a related Perspective.

‘The ability to achieve a diagnosis within 1 hour of a patient presenting to a hospital emergency department or within 1 hour of testing in a drive-through testing site could have significant benefits for both individual patients and health systems,’ they add.

In the Cepheid study, the sensitivity and specificity of the test were 100% when compared with a laboratory reference standard, and the test correctly identified all SARS-CoV-2–positive samples from previous studies.

The test can generate and display patient-specific results in 45 minutes, which the company says allows for same-day, rapid clinical management decisions.

Currently, diagnostic times in the US are between 1 and 7 days, and the country is still building its testing capacity. Critics argue that the current strategy is flawed and that the US will need to dramatically increase its testing capacity if it is to control the epidemic.

Osterholm and his team agree that the US needs to increase testing capacity, but that having rapid, accurate diagnostic tests will be a crucial part of this process.

‘We believe that the immediate deployment of this new point-of-care test for SARS-CoV-2 will be an important adjunct to existing efforts,’ they write.

A qualitative study was conducted to explore how general practitioners (GPs) and other healthcare professionals use POC diagnostics in their daily work. A total of four groups interviews were conducted: two with GPs who work at the same clinic (Group I), and two with GPs from two other clinics (Group II). The interviews were audio-recorded and data analysis was performed in accordance with the conventional content analysis method. Directed by the aim of the study five categories and 25 subcategories were identified and described.
The results showed that POC diagnostics is used in different ways depending on the nature and complexity of the symptoms, the patient’s medical history and the accessibility of other types of diagnostics. When GPs encounter uncertainty in their clinical judgement they are using POC diagnostics in different ways. Either to confirm their clinical judgement by getting objective and quantified results, to support their diagnosis by getting information about several different diseases, or to refine their clinical question by getting a focused analysis. The POC diagnostics was integrated into the workflow in different ways. Either by letting the results of the POC diagnostics alter the further actions of the GPs or by using the POC diagnostics as a starting point for the patient’s treatment. POC diagnostics was shared in three different ways. GPs shared their knowledge about the POC diagnostics with the patients or other professionals and also acknowledged that the patients shared their experiences of the POC diagnostics with other patients.
The conclusion of this study is that POC diagnostics is used as an adaptable tool that is able to meet the needs of both the GPs and the patients. samples.src: Towards definitions of critical illness and critical care using concept analysis
samples.ref: Zuwa ga ma'anar rashin lafiya mai tsanani da kulawa mai mahimmanci ta amfani da nazarin ra'ayi
samples.hyp:
: A methodological review

Journal article Full text not available from this repository.
Hazel Stewart, Susan M. Scott
Nature, Medicine, 2014
Download (1Mb)
This article has been published in Nature. Copyright Nature 2014
Background: Critical care is a relatively new specialty, and definitions of the specialty's core components are lacking. Concept analysis is a method used to clarify existing ideas and increase knowledge of a concept. It is typically conducted in five steps: 1) purpose, 2) concept analysis, 3) empirical referents, 4) case references and 5) conclusions and recommendations. A recent 'white paper' on defining critical care identified gaps in knowledge, including a lack of a consensus-based definition of critical illness and confusion about the scope of critical care. The white paper proposed concept analysis as a suitable method to address these gaps. Objectives: To explore the use of concept analysis to clarify critical illness and critical care. Methods: A methodological review of published concept analysis papers that related to critical illness and critical care. Papers were identified through searching five databases (CINAHL, EMBASE, PubMed, Scopus, and the Cochrane Library) and additional papers were identified from lists of references in relevant papers. Results: Thirteen studies met the inclusion criteria and were analysed. The majority of studies provided a limited definition or description of the concept and only one study reported following all of the steps of concept analysis. Conclusions: Concept analysis is potentially useful for clarifying critical illness and critical care. Further, and more comprehensive concept analyses are required. The results of concept analyses could inform the development of a consensus-based definition of critical illness, and provide a framework for the future development and evaluation of critical care.

We propose a definition based on the three cardinal features of sepsis, which is: i) illness severity, ii) high risk of death and iii) reversibility. Each of these three features are discussed in detail below.

Illness severity

Illness severity is a measure of the dysfunction of one or more organ systems. The best measure of illness severity in a patient with suspected sepsis is a summary of the degree of organ dysfunction, which is known as the sepsis-related organ failure (SOFA) score. The SOFA score is calculated from the degree of organ dysfunction in the respiratory, coagulation, renal, hepatic and cardiovascular systems. Each of these systems is assigned a score between 0 and 4 on the basis of the severity of the dysfunction. The total SOFA score is obtained by summing the scores for each system. A SOFA score of 0 or 1 is associated with a good outcome, a score of 2 with an increased risk of death and a score of 3 or more with a high risk of death. The SOFA score has been validated in patients with sepsis and has been shown to be useful in predicting the risk of death in patients with sepsis [1]. The SOFA score can also be calculated retrospectively, which is useful for clinical trials and studies that include patients with sepsis. A recent modification of the SOFA score, known as the qSOFA score, uses the same organs to define organ dysfunction but removes the laboratory component for simplified assessment at the bedside [2]. The qSOFA score has been validated in sub-Saharan Africa and has been shown to be useful for predicting the risk of death in patients with sepsis [3]. The SOFA and qSOFA scores are not specific to sepsis, however, and also apply to other causes of critical illness. An example of a patient with a high SOFA score is shown in Additional file 1.

The high risk of death is a fundamental feature of critical illness. The risk of death in sepsis is difficult to estimate in an individual patient because the severity of illness and the number of underlying co-morbidities vary widely between patients. The risk of death in sepsis can be estimated by using a prognostic tool that is based on a large number of patients with sepsis. We have also generated a taxonomy of the concept of self-management support. The taxonomy may assist in making the concept more explicit and aid in the development of theories of change that improve self-management support for people with chronic conditions. © 2015, authors. All rights reserved.

Self-management support (SM-S) is the assistance and guidance to enable people with long-term conditions to manage their health concerns, in order to improve health outcomes, reduce costs, and improve quality of life. SM-S is a dynamic, ongoing process that exists along a continuum. However, little consensus exists among the scientific community and the literature regarding the definition and use of the concept of SM-S. Through concept analysis of uses and definitions in the literature and among experts we have identified the defining attributes of the concepts and propose definitions that could aid clinical practice, research, and policy making. We have also generated a taxonomy of the concept of SM-S. The taxonomy may assist in making the concept more explicit and aid in the development of theories of change that improve SM-S for people with chronic conditions.
