samples.hyp:
The major strength of this study is that it is the first to examine the association between PM and HAM-D scores in a sample of depressed patients who were treated with citalopram. Although previous studies have examined the association between PM and depression in large, community-based samples11, 12, 13, 14, 15, the present study adds to the literature by including only depressed patients (with and without comorbid anxiety disorders) and by controlling for common medical and psychiatric comorbidity as well as cigarette smoking, which has been associated with both PM16, 17 and depression18, 19. In addition to addressing the aforementioned limitations of previous studies, the present study also examined the relationship between different measures of PM and depression, which is important considering the finding that different measures of PM may assess different aspects of the construct20, 21.

One limitation of the present study is that PM was measured only once at the beginning of the treatment. It is possible that some of the participants changed their PM behaviors during the 16 weeks of treatment, and thus, these data may under- or overestimate the actual association between PM behaviors at the beginning of treatment and level of depression at the end of treatment. However, it is also possible that participants’ PM behaviors at the beginning of treatment are an indication of how they will behave throughout treatment, especially since only a small number of participants (N = 30) did not complete the 16-week treatment. Replication is needed to address this limitation22, 23, 24, 25, 26. In addition, the cross-sectional nature of the study limits our ability to determine causality. It is likely that depressed individuals have more somatic complaints, including PM symptoms, than non-depressed individuals. More longitudinal research is needed to determine whether PM behaviors precipitate the development of depression or whether depression causes PM. Finally, the present study included only patients treated with citalopram, and therefore, further research is needed to determine whether the findings are generalizable to other antidepressant medication classes and to patients treated with psychotherapy alone or in combination with medication.

in the nursing literature. The study was conducted in two phases. In phase 1, 15 articles published between 1989 and 1998 on the history and development of critical care nursing were reviewed. In phase 2, 12 articles published between 1996 and 1999 that defined critical care or described the characteristics of critically ill patients were analyzed. Data from phase 1 were used to develop a preliminary list of uses and definitions of critical illness that were reviewed in phase 2. Data from phase 2 were used to identify emerging themes and to develop and test a theoretical model that reflected the researchers’ understanding of the concept critical illness. Critical illness was variously defined in terms of (a) patient characteristics (e.g., age, severity of illness), (b) disease or nosocomial process (e.g., etiology, systemic inflammatory response syndrome), (c) organ dysfunction (e.g., Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation score), (d) use of intensive care unit services or technology (e.g., more than 24% use of intensive care unit services), and (e) presence of life-threatening events (e.g., acute renal failure). Critical care was defined in terms of (a) 24-hour monitoring and support of physiologic function, (b) highly specialized nursing care and physician intervention, (c) advanced technological services and equipment, and (d) treatment and support of a critically ill patient. A model was proposed that included antecedents (e.g., early recognition of illness severity, presence of an illness with multisystem involvement), consequences (e.g., use of intensive care services, death), and sufficiency (i.e., meeting the needs of the patient).

A new study co-authored by researchers from the University of Washington School of Medicine has redefined the meaning of “critically ill” patients and their care, which could have a profound effect on how patients are treated in the United States and worldwide.

The study, published online today in the journal Critical Care, defines how best to care for patients on mechanical ventilation, the most advanced life support available outside of an intensive care unit. Patients on mechanical ventilation consume a disproportionate amount of the nations’ healthcare resources.

Maynard Miller, M.D., professor of medicine in the Division of Pulmonary and Critical Care at the UW School of Medicine and a researcher at the UW Brotman Massage Center, said the study results suggest a need to either improve the way care is delivered or, more likely, to change the way resources are allocated to patients.

“Either we are giving the wrong care to these patients or the wrong patients are getting the care, or both,” Miller said. “This tells us that we need to make some changes.”

The study looked at a type of care called early progressive care, or EPC, which involves taking patients off of maximum life support as soon as possible and giving them the highest level of care they can tolerate. The idea is to return them to a hospital ward or to a nursing home as soon as possible.

Abstract
Background
The obligate intracellular parasite Plasmodium infects liver cells of mosquitoes and humans. Altered microtubule organization is a hallmark of the parasite's intracellular stage in both vectors and mammalian cells. We previously showed that microtubule asters in parasite-infected liver cells are smaller and form fewer branches than in uninfected cells, and that this altered organization is dependent on the host cell.
Objective
To identify host factors required to maintain altered microtubule organization.
Methods
We performed a genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 knockout screen to identify genes required for maintenance of supernumerous microtubule asters in Plasmodium-infected hepatoma cells. The human hepatoma cell line, HepG2, was transfected with lentivectors containing genome-wide single-guide RNAs (sgRNAs) and co-infected with Plasmodium yoelii parasite. After selection against uninfected cells, individual sgRNA clones were isolated and retransfected, and the formation of supernumerous microtubule asters was assessed. Z-Score values were used to rank guide RNA targets, and on-target mutations were confirmed by sequencing.
Results
CRISPR screens identified 12 genes with a statistically significant depletion of sgRNA reads. Five of the genes, including ogpr1, were previously identified as important for maintenance of parasite infection. However, the remaining seven genes have not been described as important for maintenance of infection. One of these genes, CENPJ, was also depleted in a secondary screen, and on-target mutations confirmed that CENPJ was the most significantly targeted gene. Hep2 cells depleted for CENPJ protein expression formed fewer supernumerous microtubule asters, to a similar extent as observed for parasite infection. Complementation of CENPJ-knockout cells with full-length CENPJ, or the central portion of the protein, CENPJ-167, restored supernumerous microtubule aster formation.
Conclusions
We performed the first genome-wide CRISPR screen in a parasite-infected human cell line and identify CENPJ as a key regulator of microtubule organization, both in uninfected and Plasmodium-infected hepatoma cells. These findings provide new insights into the unusual organization of the apicomplexan cytoskeleton. The apicomplexa are a major group of protistan parasites, including agents of malaria (Plasmodium), giardiasis (Giardia), cryptosporidiosis (Cryptosporidium), coccidiosis (Eimeria), and toxoplasmosis (Toxoplasma gondii). One feature unique to these intracellular parasites is their invasive stage, the merozoite, a highly motile stage that invades host cells. We show that a microtubule cytoskeleton in the merozoite provides the mechanism for its extreme motility. The microtubules are arranged in a novel array that is distinct from the microtubule cytoskeleton of the host cell. Our data suggest that the microtubule array serves to generate the polarized motility that propels the merozoite into host cells. This motility is essential for the parasite, as it is required for entry into host cells, a critical step in the parasite's life cycle. We propose a model in which the microtubule array is assembled during a merozoite's final division into two daughter merozoites. This requires a novel microtubule-nucleating site and a distinct microtubule dynamics.

Scientists have long known that when a malaria parasite infects a mosquito and then infects a human, it latches onto special proteins in the red blood cells of its human host.

Now, researchers at the University of Washington and the University of Pennsylvania have determined the structure of one of those proteins, a human cell component that seems to help the parasite survive.

The findings, published today (May 17) in Nature, could lead to new treatments for malaria, which killed an estimated 627,000 people worldwide in 2017, according to the latest data from the World Health Organization (WHO). Young children in sub-Saharan Africa are especially vulnerable.

Malaria works by hitching a ride on red blood cells. When an infected mosquito bites a human, the parasite released into the human’s bloodstream latches onto the surface of red blood cells and injects part of its genetic material into the cell. The cell then replicates the parasite, eventually bursting to release new copies of the parasite into the blood.

To do this, the parasite relies on proteins in both its own makeup and in the red blood cells it has taken over. One such protein, called RON-1, is unique to the malaria parasite, but it needs a part-time job: In the 30 hours before it injects its genetic material into a red blood cell, the parasite uses RON-1 to break down the cell’s membrane to gain access to its interior.

After that, another parasite protein, called AMA-1, takes over and latches onto the surface of the red blood cell, injecting more of the parasite’s genome. That protein is the target of current malaria vaccines in development.

But RON-1 is essential to the process, too. Without it, AMA-1 cannot gain a foothold on the surface of the red blood cell.

“RON-1 is the first step in the invasion process,” said senior study author Amber J. Sheehan, an associate professor of biochemistry at the University of Washington. “Without it, there is nothing for AMA-1 to invade.”

The term cytoplasmic reticulum is often used in reference to the endoplasmic reticulum, but it also describes other internal structures that form a network, such as the mitochondrial reticulum and the nuclear envelope. The cytoplasmic reticulum is a continuous membrane structure, and it can be thought of as a system of tubes and sacs, sometimes referred to as a labyrinth. The endoplasmic reticulum is a specialized form of cytoplasmic reticulum. It is a network of tubular structures and flattened sacs that are interconnected and closely associated with the cell nucleus. The endoplasmic reticulum is involved in numerous cellular processes, including the synthesis and transport of proteins and lipids. It is also the site of calcium storage and regulation in animal cells. The endoplasmic reticulum is continuous with the outer nuclear membrane, and it is sometimes considered to be an extension of the nuclear envelope. The endoplasmic reticulum is a dynamic structure that can change in shape and function, depending on the needs of the cell. It can expand and contract, and it can even break down and reform. The endoplasmic reticulum is an important component of cellular infrastructure, and it plays a crucial role in cellular function. Its ability to store calcium and participate in protein and lipid synthesis makes it an essential part of many cellular processes. The endoplasmic reticulum is a fascinating structure that deserves further study. Its complex and dynamic nature provides insight into the inner workings of cells and the mechanisms by which they carry out their functions. As technology continues to advance, it will be interesting to see what new insights are gained about the endoplasmic reticulum and its role in cellular function.

Dr Hyde said: “We’ve shown that the microtubules are behaving very strangely in the presence of the parasite - they are not doing what they normally do in the liver cell. The next step is to look at how we can stop this from happening.”

Dr Hyde added: “Malaria is a problem that has been with us for a very long time and we have lots of different treatments and methods of trying to control it, but as we’ve seen with the rise of drug resistance we need new ways of stopping it. Professor James Chappell, from the University of Reading’s School of Biosciences, said: “The malaria parasite has an incredibly complex life cycle and the research helps to explain how the parasite manages to develop in liver cells.

Now that we know which genes are important at this stage of the parasite’s life cycle, we can start to think about how we stop the parasite from developing at this stage, which will not have serious side effects because the parasite is in the early stages of developing its reproductive organs in the liver.”

Dr Hyde said: “At the moment, malaria affects around 200 million people worldwide, causing around 400,000 deaths per year.

We’re not the first people to try to make the liver cell fight back, but what is different about this research is that we’ve actually discovered how the parasite stops the liver cell from fighting back.

The research was published in PLOS Pathogens.

This is the first study to perform a forward genetic screen in mosquitoes--the main agents of malaria transmission--to identify genes involved in resistance against this deadly parasite.

Malaria is caused by a germ called a plasmodium, which is transmitted to humans by the bite of an infected mosquito.

In the study, the scientists focused on a type of mosquito--Anopheles gambiae--which is the main vector of malaria in Africa. From larvae to adults, the team performed a genetic screen to identify genes that are important for an infection to succeed.

They found several genes that determine how severe an infection becomes. One of the genes codes for a protein that is naturally found in Anopheles gambiae mosquitoes. In other words, it makes the mosquitoes more resistant to the plasmodium parasite.

The scientists also used a reverse genetic approach, and successfully generated mosquito lines in which they deleted a specific gene. Mosquitoes in which this natural resistance gene was deleted were more susceptible to the parasite--they died faster and had higher levels of parasite reproduction.

The scientists also found that deleting another gene--which affects the immune response of the mosquitoes--had a similar effect. This natural variation in the immune response gene is found in different populations of Anopheles gambiae mosquitoes.

These findings are important for several reasons, not the least of which is that they can help us figure out how to prevent malaria in humans. All of the genes we identified are also found in other insects, including those that transmit arboviruses to humans, such as the Zika, dengue and chikungunya viruses. Arboviruses are transmitted by mosquitoes of the Aedes genus.

Our study shows that these genes are important for the mosquitoes' ability to fight infections. Future research can now focus on these genes to figure out how to weaken or disable them, which would help reduce mosquito-borne diseases in humans.

The main limitation of our study is that we focused on a single gene that is responsible for the natural resistance of mosquitoes to the malaria parasite. We did not focus on the many other genes that are involved in making the malaria parasite infect the mosquitoes in the first place. It is possible that some of the genes we identified are involved in this process.

Dr. Skovsmose wondered if the same might be true for P. vivax, the most prevalent species of human malaria parasite. P. vivax has unique biological characteristics that allow it to survive in red blood cells for extended periods of time, and to be transmitted from person to person. These characteristics make it difficult to diagnose and treat P. vivax infection, and it often causes a debilitating relapsing form of malaria.
To find out if P. vivax parasites reorganize microtubules, the researchers first exposed purified parasites to fluorescent antibodies that bind to microtubules. As shown in the accompanying video, microtubules in parasites exposed to fluorescent antibodies (in green) are organized differently than microtubules in unexposed control parasites. The researchers then performed a similar experiment, but this time exposed parasites to an inhibitor that prevents microtubule organization. Parasites exposed to the inhibitor were less capable of infecting red blood cells compared to parasites that were not exposed to the inhibitor. This experimentally demonstrated that P. vivax parasites must reorganize microtubules in order to enter red blood cells.
To visualize microtubule organization in red blood cells infected with P. vivax, the researchers developed a method to purify intact red blood cells that contain only one parasite each. Using this method, the researchers labeled purified parasites with the fluorescent antibody and then measured microtubule organization within the parasite as well as in the red blood cell in which it resided. The results revealed that P. vivax parasites reorganize microtubules to redirect cell resources into the parasite. Specifically, P. vivax parasites depolymerize cytoplasmic microtubules and incorporate them into the parasite's own microtubule network. Depolymerization of cytoplasmic microtubules generates monomeric tubulin, which is then available for use by the parasite. The parasite uses this monomeric tubulin to polymerize microtubules that are important for motility and invasion.
"By understanding how P. vivax alters the microtubule cytoskeleton of the host cell, we hope to identify new drug targets and develop novel transmission-blocking and relapse-preventing therapies," said Dr. Skovsmose.
These findings further highlight the importance of microtubules in malaria, and open new avenues for developing life-saving drugs.

The researchers also point out that the large-scale analysis of cell and organ function will provide important information for understanding how other diseases affect cells and organs. This, in turn, could lead to new drug discovery strategies.

The researchers note that the mapping of liver cell proteins will be useful for finding potential drug targets in other diseases that also affect the liver, such as hepatitis and alcoholism.

The researchers used a technology called SILAC together with quantitative mass spectrometry to determine the abundance of 2,308 unique proteins in the livers of mice infected with malaria parasites and compared them to the liver proteins of uninfected mice. Malaria infection significantly changed the abundance of 55 proteins, and 31 of these were changed in the direction consistent with increased activity of the parasite's metabolism. The researchers then used a series of bioinformatic screens to look for changes in cellular components, metabolic pathways, and interactions with other proteins. This analysis pointed to changes in the structure of the mitochondria and peroxisomes (another organelle in the cell) as well as changes in fatty acid metabolism and oxidative stress.

samples.hyp:
The most effective way to prevent infection is through bed nets, which are treated with insecticide. These nets are intended to stop mosquito bites at night, when people are most at risk of being bitten. However, in Kenya, where mosquito-borne diseases cause significant illness and death, bed nets are often used during the day, and their insecticide treatment is worn off within hours. As a result, many people are exposed to bites during the day when fewer mosquitoes are active. To investigate this issue, we examined the biting patterns of mosquitoes under different bed net treatments. We found that mosquitoes bite less frequently during the day when the nets are treated with insecticide. However, the nets also have other properties that may reduce mosquito bites during the day. Our results suggest that in areas where bed nets are used during the day, the nets should be treated with insecticide, at least every 6 months, and that people should be advised to avoid using the nets during the day.

Another is that much of the existing research focuses on models with just two drivers. We argue that polydriver models can provide new insights and help to inform policy. For example, it is likely to be more accurate to model the effect of income on food consumption as a three-way interaction between income, food prices and income expenditure rather than as a two-way interaction between income and food prices. Climate change, invasive species and human activities are threatening the survival of species in South Africa, and researchers say that these threats will worsen as the climate continues to change.

The impact of climate change is projected to make the African continent warmer and drier, with a decrease in winter rainfall in the western half of the continent and possible increases in summer rainfall in the east.

Invasive species are also expected to become a bigger problem as the climate changes.

“Climate change will cause shifts in range, timing of phenology, and abundance of native species,” said Professor Annie Dyer from the University of Cape Town’s Institute for Marine and Coastal Research.

“These changes will, in turn, provide new opportunities for alien species to establish themselves and out-compete natives, further reducing the resilience of our ecosystems.”

Researchers from the University of Cape Town, Stellenbosch University and the South African National Biodiversity Institute did a literature review of studies that have investigated the impacts of climate change, invasive species, and human activities on native species in South Africa.

They found that alien species have contributed to the extinction of 27% of threatened species in South Africa, and that climate change and human activities are also threatening the survival of many species.

The review found that invasive species have a greater impact on native species than human activities, but that both factors often have a combined effect.

The researchers say that studies that investigated the impacts of the combined effects of invasive species, climate change and human activities found that the impacts were greater than those predicted by studies that investigated the impacts of individual factors.

The team now plans to do their own studies to map the combined effects of invasive species, climate change and human activities on native species in South Africa.

They say that managers and conservationists can use their maps to make decisions about where and when to take action to reduce the impact on native species.

The international team’s study was published in the journal Diversity and Distributions.


Professor Dyer said that the next step for their international team is to investigate how the interactive effects of invasive species, climate change and human activities may change the structure of South Africa’s ecosystems.

“Once we have this data, we can predict how the combined effects of these pressures will impact native species, and work with conservation managers to develop adaptive management strategies that aim to maintain ecosystem services in the face of these changing pressures,” she said.

The quantitative analysis of SOM quality is critical to evaluate the dynamics and drivers of forest ecosystem. However, the application of conventional wet-chemical methods is limited in assessing SOM quality due to the large amounts of samples needed. In this study, we examined the major factors influencing the spatial distribution of SOM quality in a subtropical evergreen forest in southern China, based on visible near-infrared (NIR) spectroscopy and a large-scale soil sampling design. The results showed that soil pH, clay content, depth, and ecosystem age were the main determinants of SOM quality, accounting for 46.0%, 8.9%, 7.3% and 6.3% of the total variation, respectively. The prediction of SOM based on these four factors had a strong agreement with the results from the conventional wet-chemical methods (r2 = 0.726). Our results indicated that the combination of soil physicochemical properties and ecosystem attributes were the major drivers of SOM quality variation. This study provided a feasible approach to evaluate SOM quality in a large-scale forest ecosystem by combining field sampling and NIR spectroscopy, which has important implications for carbon management and assessment in large-scale forest ecosystems.

Here we assess variability in SOM and C stocks in the top 20 cm of soil in 20 miombo sites across 5 countries in the region (Zambia, Botswana, Malawi, Mozambique and Tanzania). Our study sites were chosen to represent a wide range of site conditions including different tree densities, fire frequencies, bedrock geology and climate zones. Soil samples were collected from 40 plots (2 plots per site) and analysed for soil organic carbon (SOC) using a wet oxidation method. Results show that SOC concentrations (10.4–55.3 g C kg−1 soil) and stocks (12.2–146.5 Mg C ha−1 to depth of 20 cm) exhibit large variability across sites. Multiple linear regression analysis shows that specific soil metrics related to soil texture (sand percentage, clay percentage and sand to clay ratio), tree density and fire frequency explain 58% of the variability observed in SOC concentrations across the sites. At present, miombo woodlands are under pressure from expanding human populations, increasing demand for land and land-use change. Our results indicate that managing miombo for carbon sequestration should consider soil characteristics and frequency of fire. Our results will help to improve the quantification of C stocks in miombo woodlands and support the development of appropriate management strategies for sequestering C in soil through avoiding frequent fires and maintaining or even enhancing tree cover.

Here, we show that the net carbon balance of African tropical forests is estimated to be slightly negative due to a combination of high respiration rates of the high biomass, and high carbon release from logging and forest conversion. This suggests that the potential for carbon storage through forest protection and recovery is limited for most sites, and that land-use change is the main determinant of the net carbon balance. Original text
Cut trees carefully to improve soil, say scientists studying Zambian forests
Posted at 5 Jun 2018 12:39

Cutting trees can actually help to improve the soil, scientists studying Zambian forests have found.

Forest scientists have long known that when trees are cut, new shoots grow from the stumps that can become new trees, and that the space underneath the trees is often filled by other plants.

But they have also known that when trees are cut, the quality of the soil can be affected, because the tree roots are gone.

Now researchers at the University of East Anglia (UEA) and the University of Nottingham have found that this isn't necessarily the case.

They have been studying forests in Zambia where timber trees - such as Teak - are being grown on land that was once all forest, but is now about 40 per cent forest and 60 per cent open woodland.

Timber trees are cut after 20 years, then replanted after another 20 years, so there are areas where the trees have been harvested once, twice or three times.

The researchers took soil samples from under trees that had been cut once, and compared them with samples from areas where the trees had grown continuously, and with samples from areas where the trees had been cut twice.

Dr Andrew Binks from UEA's School of Computing Sciences, who led the research, said: "We found that cutting the trees didn't necessarily have a negative impact on the soil.

"Because the trees are replanted, the researchers initially thought that the soil quality would be highest in areas where the trees had grown continuously, and decrease as the trees had been cut.

"At the start, the area where trees had been harvested three times had the worst soil, probably because it had been heavily trafficked by logging vehicles.

"But after five years, the soil quality was higher where the trees had been cut twice, and three times.

"We think this is because when the trees are first cut, the area is much lighter - it's been described as 'fluff' - and there is a lot of organic material on the surface of the soil. This allows water to get into the soil more easily, which is good for soil quality and tree growth.

"After five years, the soil in the areas where the trees had been harvested three times had fully recovered."

The researchers say the findings could help landowners and forestry companies to manage their land more effectively, and perhaps help prevent deforestation.

(Source: University of Central Florida)
A new study led by a University of Central Florida researcher shows that the topsoil in a tropical forest that was previously cleared for farming still has the ability to support plant growth, which could help countries in Africa that are struggling with high population growth and demand for food.

The study, published in the journal Land Degradation & Development, is the first to measure the amount of soil organic matter in different types of tropical forests in Africa that were previously cleared for farming. The researchers, who were led by UCF environmental scientist Delia J. Bell, studied four types of forests in Zambia that were cleared of all trees and then allowed to regenerate for three years. The land was used for farming for about 50 years prior to the study.

The researchers found that the soil in all four types of forests had a surprisingly high amount of organic matter, which is important for supporting plant growth. The findings indicate that farmers may be able to plant crops soon after clearing forests and support the plants with organic fertilizers, rather than waiting years for the land to regenerate.

“Maintaining soil organic matter is key to preventing further degradation of forest soils,” said Bell, an associate professor in UCF’s Department of Earth Sciences in the College of Sciences. “Our results suggest that there is potential to rapidly rehabilitate forested landscapes and support the growing population in Africa without a large environmental footprint.”

Bell’s team of researchers from UCF, the University of Florida and the Natural Resources and Environmental Sustainability Program at Michigan Technological University studied different types of forests in Zambia: dense eucalyptus forests that were cleared, open eucalyptus forests that were cleared, mixed hardwood and pine forests that were cleared, and a type of grassland that wasn’t technically a forest but was included in the study because it is often replaced by forests in other parts of Africa.

The researchers measured the soil organic matter 10 centimeters below the surface. They found that the organic matter in all four types of forests averaged 12.1 percent. In comparison, most non-forest soils in the world have less than 2 percent soil organic matter.

The study also found that the more light the soil received, the higher the percentage of organic matter. This is because many microorganisms that are able to break down organic matter in the soil require sunlight, Bell said.

The project aims to (i) strengthen capacities of the All Ethiopia Farmers Federation (AEFF) and Regional Agricultural Research Centers (RARC) to design, implement, and operationalize a multi-stakeholder innovation platform for chickpea; and (ii) implement activities to improve chickpea productivity and enhance market access through the platform. To achieve these objectives, the project will develop a detailed implementation plan for the chickpea multi-stakeholder innovation platform in Ethiopia, which will be based on a consultative process that builds on existing experiences and lessons learned from similar platforms and projects in other countries, as well as on the recommendations of a stakeholder analysis that will be conducted at the national and regional levels. The platform will be implemented in three regions in Ethiopia where conditions are suitable for chickpea production, and the project will focus on supporting AEFF and RARC in (i) building the platform at the national level by recruiting a national platform coordinator who will be a staff of AEFF, (ii) conducting a stakeholder analysis, (iii) developing a detailed work plan with clear activities, roles and responsibilities, and (iv) implementing the platform activities and achieving the platform goals. The platform will be managed by a National Steering Committee at the national level, which will advise AEFF and RARC on strategic directions and ensure the ownership of the platform at the national level. The platform will be implemented in three regions in Ethiopia where conditions are suitable for chickpea production. At the regional level, a Regional Management Committee will advise RARC on operational issues and ensure the ownership of the platform at the regional level. The platform approach will support AEFF and RARC in sharing knowledge on chickpea production, technologies, and best practices, as well as market information, and enable stakeholders to discuss, debate, and collaborate on challenges and opportunities along the chickpea value chain. It is expected that the platform will facilitate adoption of improved chickpea technologies and practices, increase the productivity and production of chickpea, and mediate market access for chickpea through value addition and linkages with processors and markets.


Project Type

Multi-stakeholder innovation platforms are decentralized, bottom-up approaches that bring together multiple public and private sector stakeholders that have a role and interest along the value chain of a particular sector or commodity to share knowledge and lessons learned, identify priorities, and collaborate to address challenges and opportunities. The platforms are designed to be owned and led by public sector stakeholders, with participants taking ownership of the platform at the local level.

Chickpeas are an important crop for Ethiopia, providing food security, income, and foreign exchange. However, production is subject to major yield constraints, with wide variations in yield across farmers. To address this, researchers evaluated the effects of different factors, including genetic potential, agronomic practices, and market access, on yield. This was done by collecting yield data, conducting on-farm experiments, and analyzing market statistics.

The results showed that the genetic potential of chickpeas is high, with yields up to 2.5 tons per hectare. However, most farmers achieve yields below 20% of this genetic potential. This indicates that there is significant scope for increasing yields through improved agronomic practices.

The analysis of agronomic practices showed that practices such as using improved chickpea varieties, maintaining weed control, and balancing nutrient inputs can increase yields by up to 100%. This means that if these practices are adopted, farmers can double their yields.

In addition to agronomic practices, market access also affects chickpea production. Farmers who have easier access to markets typically achieve higher yields. This is because they are more likely to use improved varieties and agronomic practices, which in turn leads to higher yields.

To fully realize the genetic potential of chickpeas and further increase yields, researchers recommend adopting improved agronomic practices and investing in market infrastructure. By doing so, chickpea production and exports from Ethiopia can be significantly enhanced, leading to better food security, income, and foreign exchange for the country.

In conclusion, both genetic potential and agronomic practices need to be optimized to maximize chickpea yields in Ethiopia. By doing so, the country can boost its production and exports of this important crop, leading to significant economic benefits.

This information helps scientists understand the potential spread and effects of the virus. Knowing the virus’s evolution can affect public health policies, such as how to best protect the public, who should be prioritized for vaccines, and what our future may look like as the virus continues to evolve. 

The SARS-CoV-2 virus, which causes COVID-19, is no exception. Scientists around the world have come together to monitor the virus’s evolution through genomic sequencing and other efforts. 

Genomic surveillance in the United States

In the United States, the National Science Foundation (NSF) and the National Institutes of Health (NIH) have partnered with the Global Virome Project to launch U.S. Genomic Surveillance for COVID-19. This effort aims to create a national network of researchers to track SARS-CoV-2 and its variants and use the data for informed public policy. The network, called the U.S. Genomic Surveillance for COVID-19, is a collaboration between academic, government, and industry scientists. 

The network’s goal is to monitor long-term community transmission and evolution here in the United States. The project will also help scientists understand how effective current vaccines are against new variants and inform decisions about future vaccines. 

The project’s initial pilot will sequence 100,000 virus genomes from across the United States. The places where sequences are sent will depend on where samples are submitted. Participating labs will analyze the data and send reports to the patients’ local health departments, which will then provide the data to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. As of June 2021, more than 5,700 virus genomes have been sequenced. 


This network of researchers is critical to understanding how the virus is changing in the United States. With this information, scientists can make informed decisions about how to best protect the public. 

Sequencing the virus

Genomic sequencing is a way to read and copy the entire DNA of an organism. In the case of the SARS-CoV-2 virus, scientists extract the virus’s RNA using a swab from the back of the nose and then use it to make many copies of itself using enzymes in a lab. Once the virus reproduces, the RNA is converted into DNA, which is then copied into what are called bacterial artificial chromosomes (BACs). The BACs are sequenced using a machine that reads the chemical code in the DNA. This produces a string of letters representing the genetic code. This code tells scientists about the virus and its proteins.

They found that the most common type of coronavirus in Uganda is similar to variants identified in the United Kingdom and South Africa, but has not yet shown the same level of resistance or transmission. The study was conducted by researchers at the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), Makerere University, and other institutions, and has been published in the American Journal of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene.

“We used to think the virus in Uganda was the one that was originally identified in Wuhan, China. But now we know this is not the case,” said senior author Dr. Waspal Sudhir, a CDC epidemiologist. “Uganda needs to be prepared for the variants that have emerged in other countries. This is a warning to conduct surveillance so we can detect these variants as early as possible.”

The researchers used a method called genome sequencing to examine the virus in 101 people hospitalized for COVID-19 in 2020. They found that 83 of the samples had a coronavirus variant that is 99.3% similar to the variant first identified in the United Kingdom. This is in contrast to the coronavirus strain that was originally detected in China.

The researchers also found that 6 of the samples had a coronavirus variant that is 99.3% similar to the variant first identified in South Africa. This particular variant may be more transmissible and may be able to evade the immune response generated by previous infection or vaccination, but more research is needed.

“Genome sequencing is a valuable tool that can be used to track the spread of viruses and guide public health decisions,” said Sudhir. “It’s also important for vaccine development and is key for understanding how viruses are evolving.”

Dr. Sudhir Sudhir is a Senior Epidemiologist at the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). His work includes providing epidemiologic support for the CDC COVID-19 response at the country and regional level in Africa. He has worked in the Division of Global HIV and TB since 2012 and joined the CDC Uganda Country Office in 2015. Prior to joining CDC, he worked for Johns Hopkins University for over 4 years as a research assistant. He has over 10 years of experience in conducting epidemiological and behavioral research and provides technical assistance to various disease programs in East and Southern Africa. Dr. Richard Lessells, another one of the authors of the study, adds: “The world needs to be prepared for future variants of concern. The authors sequence 110 SARS-CoV-2 genomes from 46 patients in Sudan, identifying 13 unique genomes, and then analyze the genomic diversity and evolutionary history of SARS-CoV-2 in this region of Africa. They find high levels of diversity, consistent with rapid expansion of early infections, and infer that SARS-CoV-2 may have been introduced into Sudan as early as March 2020. Further, they observe that the majority of sequences shared by all sub-Saharan Africa countries cluster together, distinct from the topological clusters of other countries. These data support the hypothesis that SARS-CoV-2 was introduced into each country at an early stage of the pandemic, with limited or no further importation from other countries. The authors also note some challenges in using genomic data to trace the spread of the virus, including the relatively low number of available sequences from African countries and the use of different genomic data sets with varying quality and resolution.

The authors summarize their findings as showing early and limited introduction of SARS-CoV-2 into Sudan, followed by rapid expansion, and as adding to the body of evidence that the virus spread rapidly in the early stages of the pandemic. They suggest that their results support a top-down model of SARS-CoV-2 spread in Africa, rather than the bottom-up, suggesting that African countries shared a common history of early infections, with limited or no importation from other countries. This work may be of interest to scientists studying the evolution of SARS-CoV-2 and its variants, and to public health officials working to understand the spread of the virus in different regions globally. It is important to note that the authors emphasize the need for increased sequencing efforts in African countries, to better understand the evolution of SARS-CoV-2 in this region. Overall, this paper contributes to the global effort to characterize the spread and evolution of SARS-CoV-2, with a focus on a region that has been understudied to date.

The authors’ main limitations are that they do not perform deep sequencing, which could provide greater resolution for calls of variants of concern, and that the number of samples sequenced in this study is relatively small compared to the number of confirmed COVID-19 cases in Sudan (46 samples vs. ~21,000 cases). The first book to comprehensively address the medical, legal, and social aspects of female genital alteration (FGA), What Makes a Woman? The study aims to document the reasons for and circumstances of FGM/C in three countries where the practice is prevalent: Indonesia, Ethiopia and Kenya. The study was conducted at the request of each country to gain a better understanding of the dynamics of the practice and to inform the design and implementation of effective strategies to end FGM/C.

The study used a combination of innovative methodological approaches that included in-depth interviews, focus group discussions, questionnaires, participatory mapping, life-sketch and triangulation, in three countries where FGM/C is prevalent: Indonesia, Ethiopia and Kenya. Both the clitoris and the labia minora are cut in all the variants of FGM/C practiced in Indonesia, Kenya and Ethiopia. The first cut is known as sunat in Indonesia, malec in Ethiopia and mgando in Kenya. This is the most common and least invasive type of FGM/C practiced in the three countries. The second cut is known as sunat plus in Indonesia, tumbo in Ethiopia and mgando plus in Kenya. Excision of the clitoris and the labia minora is also performed in all the three countries but the fourth type, known as sunat set, excision of the clitoris only, is only performed in Indonesia.

The practice is prevalent in 29 countries in Africa and is being practiced by increasing numbers of immigrants in Western countries. Female genital cutting/mutilation is defined differently in different countries. In the US, it is defined as the partial or total removal of the external female genitalia and any other injury to the female genital organs whether intentional or accidental. The practice is associated with beliefs about concepts of the acceptable appearance of women, and is believed to be important for future sexual and reproductive health of girls and women, and serve hygienic, social, and religious functions. Female genital cutting/mutilation is generally performed by traditional cutters in a non-medical setting, and may involve the use of unsterile equipment. The practice is most commonly performed on girls younger than 5 years of age. The consequences of the practice include severe bleeding, infection, pain, shock, and death. Adverse long-term consequences include infertility, dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, urinary problems, obstructed labor, and increased risk of cesarean section. The practice is a violation of the human rights of millions of girls and women. The removal of genital tissue that is vital to normal sexual functioning should not be performed. Efforts are underway to eliminate the practice. These include implementation of international treaties, national laws and policies, and awareness campaigns at the local and national levels. Such efforts need to be intensified to end female genital cutting/mutilation.

However, the evidence on the impact of their communication and information sharing is limited. This study assessed the impact of a training programme for health workers in primary health care centres in Somalia on their communication with girls and women about FGM/C, and girls’ and women’s subsequent decisions about FGM/C.

This study was embedded within a cluster randomized trial evaluating the impact of the training programme compared to usual care on FGM/C prevalence. Qualitative process evaluation methods were used to assess the impact of the training on communication and decision-making. In-depth interviews and observations were conducted with 28 girls and women who attended the health facilities, and 11 health workers and clinic managers at follow-up 6 and 12 months after the intervention.

Health workers provided information about FGM/C and encouraged girls and women to ask questions. The training supported health workers to deliver this information clearly and sensitively. Health workers’ positive communication about FGM/C was associated with girls’ and women’s intentions to prevent FGM/C.

This study suggests that a training programme for health workers in communication skills and provision of information about FGM/C may be an effective component of a strategy to reduce FGM/C prevalence. Further research should explore the impact of health worker communication on girls’ and women’s decisions and explore other strategies to increase the capacity of health workers to communicate about FGM/C.

The World Health Organization (WHO) defines female genital mutilation (FGM) as any procedure that involves altering or injuring the female genitals for non-medical reasons. This practice has been widely performed in 29 African countries and in Yemen, where around 85 million girls and women have undergone FGM. The tradition is also practiced in some countries in Asia and the Middle East.

Female genital mutilation is often performed on girls aged between four and 14, although in some countries the procedure is performed on newborn girls. The procedure is usually carried out by traditional birth attendants or circumcisers, who are often members of the girl’s family.

The practice of female genital mutilation has significant health consequences, both short and long term. These include severe bleeding, infection, shock and death. In the long term, FGM can cause difficulties in pregnancy and childbirth. It can also affect girls’ mental health, as the procedure is typically performed without anesthesia or under unhygienic conditions.

The model they used looks at four different levels – individual, relationship, community and structural. It found that both individual and community factors were involved. Individual factors included girls and women who saw FGM as a right, and a way to enhance female cleanliness. Community factors included social pressure, the belief that FGM is a tradition and a social norm, the ease of access to hospitals and clinics to perform FGM, and the belief that FGM is required by religion.

The researchers say that some women and girls said they had FGM because their mothers told them it was their responsibility to continue the tradition. The study also found that a high number of girls and women said they believed FGM had health benefits.

The researchers point out that some communities have successfully ended FGM. They say that this supports the idea that FGM can end, even in communities with a strong belief that it should continue.

samples.src: Reproductive Hormones Imbalance, Germ Cell Apoptosis, Abnormal Sperm Morphophenotypes and Ultrastructural Changes in Testis of African Giant Rats (Cricetomys gambianus, Waterhouse, 1840) Exposed to Sodium Metavanadate Intoxication
samples.ref: Rashin Daidaiton Ƙwayoyin Halitta na Haihuwa, Mutuwar Ƙwayoyin Sel, Maniyyin Halittun Morphophenotypes da Canje-canje na Tsare-tsare a cikin Gwajin Ɓerayen Dinka (Cricetomys gambianus, Waterhouse, 1840) da aka Bayyanar ga maye gurbin Sodium Metavanadate
samples.hyp:
The effects of sodium metavanadate (NaVO3) on the reproductive system of male African giant rats (Cricetomys gambianus) were investigated. Twenty-one rats were randomly assigned to three groups: the first group (n=7) received drinking water (control), the second (n=7) was administered NaVO3 at a dose of 10 mg/L for 90 days, and the third (n=7) was administered NaVO3 at a dose of 30 mg/L for 90 days. The body weight of rats from the control group was higher than that of rats from treated groups (p<0.05). Testicular relative weights of rats from treated groups were lower than those of the control group (p<0.05). Marked histological changes were observed in the testes of rats treated with NaVO3. The seminiferous tubule lumens were atrophied, and the spermatogonia and spermatocytes were reduced in number. Sertoli cells were enlarged with a pale-staining nucleus and vacuolated cytoplasm. Leptotene and pachytene stages of meiosis were reduced. The interstitial tissue was infiltrated with a large number of small round cells, which were positive for ascites fluid and terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT) and negative for KiM1.18. Apoptotic germ cells were detected using TdT-mediated dUTP nick end labeling (TUNEL) and were found in the seminiferous tubules of all treated rats. Electron microscopy revealed that the main changes in the testis of rats treated with NaVO3 were the appearance of cytoplasmic vacuoles in the spermatogonia, spermatocytes, and round spermatids, as well as detachment of spermatids from the spermatogonia. We conclude that NaVO3 induces testicular toxicity in the African giant rat, and that the damage is associated with germ cell apoptosis and pachytene meiotic arrest.

Keywords: Cricetomys gambianus; sodium metavanadate; testis; seminiferous tubule; germ cell; apoptosis; ultrastructure

This is due to the increase in the vanadium mining and processing in several countries. Vanadium is a metal that is widely used in steel manufacturing, and in the petrochemical industry. The aim of this study was to assess the level of vanadium in hair of workers in a vanadium processing factory in South Africa and to determine the factors that may contribute to increased vanadium exposure. A cross-sectional study was conducted on 160 workers of a vanadium processing factory in South Africa. The levels of vanadium in hair of the workers were measured and information on the personal and job-related factors that may increase exposure to vanadium was assessed by means of a questionnaire. The results showed that: 1) the level of vanadium in hair of the workers increases with increasing length of employment at the factory, 2) there is a significant difference in the level of vanadium in hair of the different groups of workers, and 3) there is a significant correlation between the level of vanadium in hair and the number of years since the commencement of the factory. The findings of this study suggest that the level of vanadium exposure increases with increasing length of employment at the factory. This could be an indication that the level of exposure to vanadium is higher among long-service workers. There is, however, a need for more sophisticated methods of exposure assessment that can measure the level of exposure to vanadium at individual level.

samples.hyp:
In the environment, it exists in multiple forms that can be difficult to distinguish using common analytical techniques. This factsheet defines bioavailability and discusses its importance in determining the environmental risk of this metal. It then describes several field and laboratory methods that can be used to determine the bioavailability of this metal in the environment. Finally, cautionary notes are provided regarding use of these methods.


The term bioavailability refers to the portion of a contaminant that is available to be taken up by living organisms, including humans. Not all portions of a contaminant are available to be taken up to the same degree. For example, the portion of a contaminant that is dissolved in water is often more available than the portion attached to particles. The amount of a contaminant that is available to be taken up by organisms depends on the chemical form of the contaminant, the properties of the particles to which it is attached (if any), and the characteristics of the environment.

The bioavailability of a contaminant is important to consider because it affects whether and how much an organism will be exposed and ultimately how toxic the contaminant will be. For example, if only a small portion of a contaminant is available, an organism may not be exposed to enough to cause a biological effect, even if the contaminant itself is toxic at the concentrations present. The opposite is also true: a contaminant with very high bioavailability in a particular environment can result in harmful effects in organisms exposed to relatively low concentrations. In addition, bioavailability can change over time. For example, as particles to which a contaminant is attached settle, the amount of contaminant that is dissolved in the water may increase, resulting in increased bioavailability and potentially increased exposure.

This factsheet is focused on the bioavailability of metals. It should be recognized, however, that bioavailability is a general term that can also be used to describe the availability of other types of contaminants, such as petroleum products or pesticides. In addition, some of the methods discussed below to characterize bioavailability are specific to metals while others are more general.

The bioavailability of a metal in the environment can have important implications for human health and the environment. Metals can be persistent and mobile in the environment and some are known to cause acute or chronic health effects in humans (see the fact sheets for individual metals for more information). Thus, determining the bioavailability of metals is important for assessing both human health and ecological risks.

samples.src: The current study was conducted to investigate the reproductive toxicity of sodium metavanadate (SMV) in male African giant rats.
samples.ref: An gudanar da binciken na yanzu don bincikar ƙarfin gubar haifuwa na sodium metavanadate (SMV) a cikin Ɓerayen Dinka.
samples.hyp:
The rats were exposed to SMV at 200, 400, 600, 800 and 1000 mg/kg body weight via oral gavage for 90 consecutive days. The control group received distilled water. Animals were pair-housed throughout the study and were checked for adverse clinical signs and mortality on a daily basis. At the end of the study, animals were euthanized, and the weights of the testes, epididymis, prostate and seminal vesicles were recorded. Testes were weighed in combination with the epididymis (testes with epididymis). Histopathological examination of the testes, epididymis, prostate and seminal vesicles were performed. Sperm parameters (sperm count, motility and morphology) were assessed in the caudal region of the vasa deferentia. The results showed that oral administration of SMV significantly (p<0.05) reduced body weight, body weight gain, food consumption and food conversion efficiency. SMV also caused a significant (p<0.05) decrease in the weights of the testes, epididymis, prostate and seminal vesicles. SMV induced a significant (p<0.05) decrease in the sperm count, motility and morphology. Oral administration of SMV caused hypospadias, atrophy of the testes, epididymis, prostate and seminal vesicles. The present study indicates that SMV is potentially toxic to male reproductive system in African giant rats.

Researchers say metal found in polluted air makes rats infertile

A new study shows that rats exposed to air containing copper and zinc become infertile.

The study, conducted by researchers at the University of Montreal and the University of Quebec, used copper and zinc sulfate to pollute the air in a stainless steel chamber. Male and female rats were then placed in the chamber for eight hours a day for four weeks.

After the four weeks, the researchers put the male rats in a new clean chamber with clean female rats. The researchers found that 44 percent of the rats were infertile, meaning they failed to mate or produce at least one litter within 10 weeks.

The infertile rats were not good fathers. The fertile rats, on the other hand, were good fathers. They spent more time with their offspring and were more willing to share food with their litter.

The study also found that even when the rats were exposed to copper and zinc for only one day, their sperm motility decreased.

The researchers believe that the same can happen with humans.

"Since humans are exposed to a combination of metals in our daily lives, the effect of a mixture of metals cannot be ignored," said the study authors.

The study was published online in the journal Human Reproduction.

Previous studies have shown that air pollution can have harmful effects on fertility. In this new study, the researchers wanted to find out whether specific metals in polluted air affect sperm quality and function.

The researchers believe that metal particles in the air we breathe can end up in our sperm, reducing its quality and function.

For the study, the researchers examined reproductive data from 61 published studies in the U.S. that included 10,000 men between the ages of 18 and 59.

They found that sperm quality and quantity declined with age. However, the rate of decline was slower than previously thought, the researchers said.

Overall, the researchers found that sperm concentration was 1.6% lower for each year of age after age 30.

“Sperm quality and quantity are dependent on many different factors, and our results do not suggest that older men are unable to have children with their partners,” Ceccato said.

The changes may be the result of environmental factors, the researchers said. Previous studies have linked environmental factors, including increased exposure to chemicals in the environment and lifestyle factors, with fertility problems.

“While our study does not identify the specific environmental factors that may be responsible for the observed changes, previous studies have suggested that chemicals in our food and water, as well as our lifestyle, may play an important role,” Ceccato said.

The researchers hope that further studies will help identify the environmental factors that may be responsible for the changes in sperm quality and quantity with age.

The present study was designed to investigate the toxic effects of vanadium on the structure and function of rat heart mitochondria. The present work was also aimed to study the protective role of melatonin against vanadium induced mitochondrial dysfunction in rat heart. Different groups of rats were administered with sodium metavanadate (Na2O2V2) at a single dose of 100 mg/kg body weight for 15 days and melatonin at a single dose of 20 mg/kg body weight for 4 weeks. Thereafter, the animals were sacrificed and their hearts were removed, perfused and incubated with 1% bovine heart mitochondrial suspension in 2.5 ml of incubation medium (IM) containing 0.5% bovine serum albumin. The incubated heart mitochondrial suspension was used to perform the assay for determination of mitochondrial swelling by measuring the release of lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) activity. Melatonin was found to significantly (p<0.0001) reduce vanadium induced mitochondrial dysfunction in rat heart. Vanadium treated rats showed 49.97% reduction (p<0.0001) in mitochondrial swelling as compared to control group of rats. Melatonin treatment showed 49.24% (p<0.0001) reduction in vanadium induced mitochondrial dysfunction. The present study thus concludes that melatonin acts as a protective agent against vanadium induced mitochondrial dysfunction in rat heart.

The aim of this study was to identify the homegarden plant species in a rural community in Ethiopia and to assess the cultural importance of these species. A secondary aim was to investigate the influence of environmental factors on the cultural use of homegarden plants. Ethno botanical surveys were conducted in four villages in the Gishe Wereda of the North West part of Ethiopia. The cultural importance of the homegarden plants was assessed using the cultural importance index (CII). Correlation and multiple regression analyses were used to investigate the relationship between environmental factors and cultural use of homegarden plants. In total, 61 homegarden plant species from 25 families were identified in the study area. The most important species were Zanthoxylum gilletii (CII = 49.9), Ekebergia pannosa (CII = 49.4), Ficus sur (CII = 48.7), Ficus thonningii (CII = 48.0), and Millettia pinnata (CII = 47.6). The results of the correlation and regression analyses showed that environmental factors have a significant influence on the cultural use of homegarden plants. The ethno botanical study identified a number of homegarden plant species that play an important role in the cultural life of the indigenous people in the study area. The results could be used for future conservation and development programs in the area.

Homegardens are a significant source of food and other products to millions of people in the tropics (Garcia et al., 2011). Homegardens are often a complex mixture of native and exotic species, which are grown alone or in combination with other crops (Warner, 2014). The study of homegardens has focused on their value for food and economic security (Altangerel et al., 2015; Mlingwa et al., 2016), water management (Eitzel et al., 2017), biodiversity conservation (Valderrama et al., 2012), and health (Galan et al., 2016). These studies have stressed the importance of homegardens as a source of fruit for home consumption and income from sales of surplus production. Less attention has been given to the significance of the beauty, shade, spiritual healing, and other non-essential, but culturally important, aspects of homegardens (Galan et al., 2016; Mlingwa et al., 2016). The study reported here addresses this gap. Our specific objectives were to (1) document the composition of homegardens in the Mount Elgon region of Kenya, (2) determine the significance of non-essential cultural values of homegardens, and (3) assess the relationship between floristic composition and cultural significance. We hope our results will provide a foundation for the improvement of homegardens, and therefore the livelihoods, of small-scale farmers in the region.

In each kebele, villages were stratified by agroecological zone (high, medium, low altitude), and the number of sampled households was allocated to each stratum proportional to its population size. Next, in each stratum, sampled villages were divided into segments of equal population size. For each segment, a list of all households was compiled, and one household was randomly selected from the list using a random number table. All eligible individuals (aged 15–59 years old) in the sampled households were listed, and every 4th individual was selected for interview using a random number table (1–4). If the selected individual proved to be absent, the next individual in sequence was interviewed. If the second one was also absent, another household was randomly selected, and all eligible individuals in that household were listed and interviewed in order of age (oldest first). For women aged 15–49 years old, an additional interview was conducted with the husband, and for married men aged 15–59 years old, an additional interview was conducted with the wife. For selected households, a 30 km walking route was mapped around the household. If more than one household was selected in a village, a common route was mapped that touched each sampled household.

However, this knowledge is often not formally acknowledged or documented. In this study, we aimed to analyze and assess the knowledge of the Shuar, a tribal population in Ecuador, on properties of plants used in their daily diet. We conducted 20 semi-structured interviews to (i) identify the species grown in homegardens and (ii) analyze and evaluate the knowledge of the Shuar on the properties of the 20 most cultivated plants. We focused on properties that indicate potential medicinal and nutritional values. We also analyzed the agreement or disagreement of this traditional knowledge with scientific data available in the literature. We found that the traditional knowledge of the Shuar on properties of some plants was in agreement with scientific data. The highest consensus was found for Hancornia noxoides (Olacaceae), Murumuru (Buriachia edulis, Arecaceae), and Inga feuillee (Fabaceae), which are known in Ecuador as “tree butter”, “peanut”, and “keki banana”, respectively. This is the first study that evaluates the properties of the seeds of B. edulis and the leaves of I. feuillee . We also found some disagreement between the traditional knowledge of the Shuar and scientific results. For example, the Shuar consider M. edulis a nutritious plant due to its high fat content, while scientific data shows that it contains toxic cardenolides in its leaves and seeds. In addition, some plants known to science were unknown to the Shuar or were used in a different way. For example, the Shuar people were unaware of the medicinal properties of Guayaibí ( Cordia trichotoma , Boraginaceae) and the wood of H. noxoides , which is used to make musical instruments. In this study, we concluded that the traditional knowledge of the Shuar people is consistent with scientific data for most evaluated plants, but more efforts are needed to avoid losing this valuable knowledge connected to the use of plants in their homegardens.

The project ‘Documenting Ethiopia’s Walled Gardens: A Digital Archive and Online Directory of a Vanishing Landscape’ aims to create an online directory, including digital records and photographs, of walled gardens in Ethiopia. Walled gardens are very common in Ethiopia, and were originally used for growing vegetables for consumption by the household and for medicinal purposes. Today, they represent one of the last examples of a traditional form of food production and storage that is rapidly disappearing. The project aims to collect data and photographs of walled gardens in various regions of Ethiopia, with a total of 120 gardens in 3 regions. The project will contribute to the conservation of this unique form of food production and storage, as well as increase food security in Ethiopia. The project is being conducted by Cornell University Library, in collaboration with Addis Ababa University.

The project aims to achieve the following:

  1. Document ethnobotanical uses of plants in walled gardens.
  2. Digitize historical and ethnobotanical materials related to walled gardens at the National Herbarium in Addis Ababa.
  3. Document 120 walled gardens in Addis Ababa, Tigray, and Wolayita through field research.
  4. Create an online archive that includes images of walled gardens and ethnobotanical information.
Project location

Woreda 1, Addis Ababa, Ethiopia

Woreda 3, Addis Ababa, Ethiopia

Tigray, Ethiopia

Wolayita, Ethiopia

Project description

The walled gardens (also called kitchen gardens and rooftop gardens) are very common in Ethiopia, though little is known about them. This project will result in the first documentation of these gardens, and in the long run will contribute towards their conservation. The project team will document 120 gardens in and around Addis Ababa, Tigray, and Wolayita, and will create an online archive that includes information about the garden, ethnobotanical uses of the plants, and 1-2 high resolution photographs of the garden. The project team is working closely with the National Herbarium at the National University of Ethiopia in Addis Ababa. There, the team will document ethnobotanical uses of plants in the walled gardens, and will digitize historical and ethnobotanical materials related to walled gardens.

But they say little is known about the exact number of plant species being used, their origin, and their potential to solve some of the country’s most pressing problems, such as soil erosion.

“Plants have been very important for Ethiopians for thousands of years,” said Lise Volpato, a postdoctoral researcher in the University of British Columbia’s (UBC) department of botany and co-founder of the Botany Photo Finder website. “People have used plants for food, for medicine, for shelter, for clothing and for a whole range of other things. And plants have been an important part of their culture and their art.”

Volpato is the lead author of a new study that aims to better understand the role plants play in Ethiopians’ daily lives. The study, “The ethnobotany of Ethiopia: A review of the current literature and recommendations for future research,” was published recently in the journal Economic Botany.

Volpato said very few ethnobotanical studies of Ethiopian plants have been conducted. Ethnobotany is the study of the relationship between people and plants.

“Ethnobotanical studies look at how people use plants in their culture and what parts of the plant they use and why,” she explained. “Scientists do surveys and ask lots of questions, like ‘What is this plant used for?’ ‘Do you know where it grows?’ and ‘Do you know why it’s used for that?’ They document all these different uses and then try to identify the plant species being used.”

Volpato said this type of research is important because it can help scientists identify plants that could be used to solve real-world problems.

“Sometimes people know about plants that could be useful, but they may not know the scientific name for them,” she said. “If we can document this information, then we can look at how that plant works and see if it’s effective for the problem at hand. We can then look at how we can use that plant to help with that problem.”

The study reviewed 83 papers that included information about plants used for a range of purposes in Ethiopia. The papers were published between 1896 and 2016, with the majority written in the 1960s and ’70s.

This tool was developed to identify which vegetable varieties are actually grown by small-scale vegetable growers in Ethiopia.
